analysis.scope_and_question: Rabies virus and rabies disease. The study focuses on health-facility readiness and provider-perceived barriers and facilitators to animal-bite management in Mangalore, India. The central question is how facility readiness and provider perspectives affect the delivery of complete rabies post-exposure care.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A convergent mixed-methods study was conducted in six urban primary health centres (PHCs) and one district-hospital animal-bite clinic. Facility readiness was assessed using a checklist adapted from NAPRE 2030 and IPHS 2022. Nine providers (five medical officers and four staff nurses) were interviewed purposively. Quantitative and qualitative data were analysed separately and integrated through a joint display and narrative triangulation.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: In the sampled urban facilities, point-in-time vaccine and cold-chain readiness coexisted with important gaps in HRIG access, wound-washing infrastructure, staffing, documentation and continuity of supply. Facility-level strengthening and coordinated referral pathways are required to improve delivery of complete rabies post-exposure care.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Evidence exploring healthcare provider’s perspectives alongside facility preparedness remains limited. Stock-register review showed at least one ARV stock-out during the preceding six months in 2/6 PHCs (33.3%); the district hospital reported none. HRIG and a designated wound-washing station were unavailable in all 6/6 PHCs (0%) but available at the district-hospital clinic. Nursing staffing met the applicable norm in 2/6 PHCs (33.3%) and at the district hospital.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Referral burden, intermittent vaccine supply, competing staff responsibilities, wage-related non-adherence and local adaptive practices were identified as key issues affecting provider adherence to rabies post-exposure protocols.

analysis.summary_en: This mixed-methods study examines health-facility readiness and provider-perceived barriers to animal-bite management in Mangalore, India, focusing on rabies virus and rabies disease. The study highlights that while anti-rabies vaccine (ARV) is physically available in all sampled facilities, there are gaps in human rabies immunoglobulin (HRIG) access, wound-washing infrastructure, staffing, and continuity of supply. Provider interviews reveal challenges such as referral burden, intermittent vaccine supply, and wage-related non-adherence. The findings suggest that facility-level strengthening and coordinated referral pathways are essential to improve the delivery of complete rabies post-exposure care. The study underscores the need for targeted research and practice improvements to address these gaps in rabies management.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 狂犬病病毒 和 狂犬病 疾病。该研究的重点是印度门格洛尔的卫生设施准备情况以及提供者认为的动物咬伤管理障碍和促进因素。核心问题是设施准备情况和提供者的观点如何影响完整的 狂犬病 暴露后护理的提供。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 在六个城市初级卫生中心(PHC)和一个地区医院动物咬伤诊所进行了一项综合混合方法研究。使用改编自 NAPRE 2030 和 IPHS 2022 的清单评估设施准备情况。有目的地采访了九名提供者(五名医务人员和四名护士)。定量和定性数据分别进行分析,并通过联合展示和叙事三角测量进行整合。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 在抽样的城市设施中,时间点 疫苗 和冷链准备情况与 HRIG 通道、伤口清洗基础设施、人员配备、文件和供应连续性方面的重大差距并存。需要加强设施级别和协调转诊途径,以改善完整的 狂犬病 暴露后护理的提供。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 探索医疗保健提供者的观点以及设施准备情况的证据仍然有限。库存登记审查显示,2/6 的初级卫生保健机构 (33.3%) 在过去 6 个月内至少有 1 次抗逆转录病毒药物缺货;地区医院没有报告任何情况。所有 6/6 的初级卫生保健中心 (0%) 均没有 HRIG 和指定的伤口清洗站,但在区医院诊所有。2/6 的初级卫生保健中心 (33.3%) 和地区医院的护理人员配置符合适用标准。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 转介负担、间歇性 疫苗 供应、相互竞争的员工责任、与工资相关的不遵守和当地适应性做法被确定为影响提供者遵守 狂犬病 暴露后协议的关键问题。

Quantitative and qualitative data were analysed separately and integrated through a joint display and narrative triangulation.
analysis_en.consensus_and_key_conclusions: In the sampled urban facilities, point-in-time vaccine and cold-chain readiness coexisted with important gaps in HRIG access, wound-washing infrastructure, staffing, documentation and continuity of supply. Facility-level strengthening and coordinated referral pathways are required to improve delivery of complete rabies post-exposure care.
analysis_en.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Evidence exploring healthcare provider’s perspectives alongside facility preparedness remains limited. Stock-register review showed at least one ARV stock-out during the preceding six months in 2/6 PHCs (33.3%); the district hospital reported none. HRIG and a designated wound-washing station were unavailable in all 6/6 PHCs (0%) but available at the district-hospital clinic. Nursing staffing met the applicable norm in 2/6 PHCs (33.3%) and at the district hospital.
analysis_en.research_and_practice_implications: Referral burden, intermittent vaccine supply, competing staff responsibilities, wage-related non-adherence and local adaptive practices were identified as key issues affecting provider adherence to rabies post-exposure protocols.

papers.title_zh: 印度门格洛尔的卫生设施准备情况和提供者认为的动物咬伤管理障碍和促进因素:一项混合方法研究
papers.source_body_en: Abstract Rabies remains a global fatal disease yet fully preventable zoonotic disease, with India accounting for a substantial share of global deaths. Timely and full post exposure prophylaxis following animal bites is crucial, but its effective delivery depends mainly on the readiness of primary healthcare systems. However, evidence exploring healthcare provider’s perspectives alongside facility preparedness remains limited. We conducted a convergent mixed-methods study in six urban primary health centres (PHCs) and one district-hospital animal-bite clinic. Facility readiness was assessed using a checklist adapted from NAPRE 2030 and IPHS 2022, and nine providers (five medical officers and four staff nurses) were interviewed purposively. Quantitative and qualitative data were analysed separately and integrated through a joint display and narrative triangulation. Anti Rabies Vaccine (ARV) was physically available in all 6/6 PHCs (100%) and at the district-hospital clinic on the assessment date. However, stock-register review showed at least one ARV stock-out during the preceding six months in 2/6 PHCs (33.3%); the district hospital reported none. Human Rabies Immunoglobulin (HRIG) and a designated wound-washing station were unavailable in all 6/6 PHCs (0%) but available at the district-hospital clinic. Nursing staffing met the applicable norm in 2/6 PHCs (33.3%) and at the district hospital. Interviews explained referral burden, intermittent vaccine supply, competing staff responsibilities, wage-related non-adherence and local adaptive practices. In the sampled urban facilities, point-in-time vaccine and cold-chain readiness coexisted with important gaps in HRIG access, wound-washing infrastructure, staffing, documentation and continuity of supply. Facility-level strengthening and coordinated referral pathways are required to improve delivery of complete rabies post-exposure care.
papers.abstract_zh: 摘要 狂犬病 仍然是一种全球致命疾病,但完全可以预防的人畜共患疾病,其中印度在全球死亡人数中占很大比例。动物咬伤后及时、全面的暴露后预防至关重要,但其有效实施主要取决于初级卫生保健系统的准备情况。然而,探索医疗保健提供者观点以及设施准备情况的证据仍然有限。我们在六个城市初级卫生中心(PHC)和一个地区医院动物咬伤诊所进行了一项融合混合方法研究。使用改编自 NAPRE 2030 和 IPHS 2022 的清单评估设施准备情况,并有目的地采访了九名提供者(五名医务人员和四名护士)。定量和定性数据分别进行分析,并通过联合展示和叙事三角测量进行整合。在评估之日,抗 狂犬病 疫苗 (ARV) 在所有 6/6 初级卫生保健中心 (100%) 和地区医院诊所均可用。然而,库存登记审查显示,2/6 的初级卫生保健机构 (33.3%) 在过去 6 个月内至少有 1 次抗逆转录病毒药物缺货;地区医院没有报告任何情况。所有 6/6 初级卫生保健中心 (0%) 都没有人 狂犬病 免疫球蛋白 (HRIG) 和指定的伤口清洗站,但在区医院诊所有。2/6 的初级卫生保健中心 (33.3%) 和地区医院的护理人员配置符合适用标准。访谈解释了转介负担、间歇性 疫苗 供应、相互竞争的员工责任、与工资相关的不遵守情况以及当地的适应性做法。在抽样的城市设施中,时间点 疫苗 和冷链准备情况与 HRIG 通道、伤口清洗基础设施、人员配备、文件和供应连续性方面的重大差距并存。需要加强设施级别和协调转诊途径,以改善完整的 狂犬病 暴露后护理的提供。

news.content_title: Increase in Reported Human Rabies Exposures and Rabies Post-exposure Prophylaxis Administration
news.content: News Flash Increase in Reported Human Rabies Exposures and Rabies Post-exposure Prophylaxis Administration Kansas Health Alert Network (KS-HAN) Posted on September 15, 2026 Summary The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Kansas Department of Health and Environment (KDHE) are issuing a Health Alert Network (HAN) Health Advisory in response to recent increases in encounters with potentially rabid animals, primarily bats in Kansas, and the associated need to perform a rabies risk assessment. Health departments and healthcare providers should be aware of the importance of rabies risk assessments before administering rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). Clinicians and healthcare facilities should ensure that rabies PEP is administered only when appropriate and that rabies vaccine and human rabies immune globulin (HRIG) is always administered according to ACIP recommendations. Background Rabies is a zoonotic viral disease that is nearly 100% fatal but is preventable when PEP is given appropriately before patient symptoms start. An infected animal can spread rabies to humans and other animals through bites, scratches, or oral secretions. Rabies primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to encephalitis and death if medical care is not received soon after exposure and before symptoms start. The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) post-exposure prophylaxis to prevent human rabies recommendations outline rabies exposure assessment, wound care, vaccination, and immunoglobulin dosing. Following a potential rabies exposure, it is important for a health official familiar with animal rabies epidemiology to help assess exposure risk and determine if a patient might need PEP. Two rabies vaccines, Imovax ® (HDCV) and RabAvert ® (PCECV), and two HRIG products, KEDRABTM and HyperRabTM , are licensed for use in people in the United States. Each year, an estimated 1.4 million people in the United States seek medical care after animal contact and undergo evaluation, and approximately 100,000 people receive rabies PEP following a potential exposure. According to weekly pharmacy data as of September 2, 2026, utilization for the two rabies vaccines and the two rabies immunoglobulins licensed in the United States has increased by an estimated 33% and 76%, respectively, compared with the same period last year. Although there is currently no shortage of human rabies vaccine or human rabies immunoglobulin in the United States, it is important for clinicians to administer PEP appropriately because errors in rabies risk assessment and PEP administration could result in unnecessary treatment (e.g., additional doses of vaccine or HRIG), potential adverse effects, and avoidable costs. A typical course of PEP can cost between $11,000 and $14,000 per person. Following rabies PEP administration guidance helps ensure that lifesaving vaccines are available for persons who need it and extraneous costs are avoided. Correct rabies PEP administration depends on the patient’s previous rabies vaccination status. For persons who have never been vaccinated against rabies, PEP should always include HRIG and vaccine. HRIG is administered once when PEP is initiated; if initially omitted, HRIG may be administered through the date of a patient’s third vaccination dose (day 7). HRIG is infiltrated into and around all identifiable wounds to the extent anatomically feasible, and any remaining volume is administered intramuscularly at a site distant from the first vaccine dose. Rabies vaccine is administered intramuscularly in the deltoid area (for adults) or in the deltoid or anterolateral thigh (for children) on days 0, 3, 7, and 14. Persons who were previously vaccinated against rabies should receive vaccine on days 0 and 3 and should not receive HRIG. Rabies vaccine is not administered in the gluteal area. HRIG and the first vaccine dose are never administered in the same syringe or anatomical site. Other recommendations apply to persons with altered immunity. Commonly reported errors in rabies PEP administration include: Administering rabies vaccine in the gluteal area. Failing to infiltrate HRIG into and around all identifiable wounds to the extent anatomically feasible. Administering HRIG and vaccine in the same syringe or anatomical site. Forgetting to give HRIG to someone who needs it. Administering HRIG to a person who was previously vaccinated against rabies. Misclassifying previous vaccination history or immune status, resulting in omitted or unnecessary biologics doses. Using an incorrect rabies vaccine schedule. Unnecessarily restarting the rabies vaccine series after a schedule deviation. Healthcare Provider Actions Requested 1. To encourage appropriate rabies PEP assessment and administration: Information on rabies epidemiology in Kansas and resources for clinicians are available on the KDHE rabies website . Contact your local health department or the 24/7 KDHE Epidemiology Hotline at 877-427-7317, option 5 for consultation on individual situations when needed. Be familiar with the complete CDC rabies post-exposure prophylaxis guidance. Learn common errors when administering rabies PEP and what to do to correct them. Ask patients about immunocompromising conditions, immunosuppressive medications, and prior rabies vaccination both in the United States and outside the country . Consult your hospital pharmacist if you have questions about rabies PEP administration for an individual patient. 2. Provide immediate wound care. Immediately and thoroughly wash each wound with water and soap (or water alone). If available, irrigate wounds with a virucidal agent such as povidone-iodine solution . Do not close the wound until HRIG has been administered. 3. Confirm that a rabies exposure occurred and that PEP is indicated. Promptly conduct a rabies risk assessment that considers the risk of rabies in the animal, the circumstances that led to the exposure, if the animal had any clinical signs consistent with rabies, and the type and severity of the wound. If needed, public health officials can help conduct the risk assessment. To help guide risk assessments, a CDC tool is available to help evaluate the risk of rabies in animals that are unable to undergo testing or observation periods. Verify prior rabies vaccination history to determine if the patient previously completed pre- or post-exposure prophylaxis. Check with your local public health authority to determine if suspect rabies exposures and animal bites are reportable. These are NOT reportable to KDHE. In general, PEP is not recommended when the animal is available for a 10-day post-exposure observation, rabies test results are negative, or health officials determine the exposure does not pose a rabies risk. 4. Administer HRIG only if the patient has not previously received rabies vaccine: A person is considered vaccinated for rabies if they have received either a full pre-exposure or post-exposure prophylaxis series OR a partial series followed by documentation of a serologic titer ≥0.5 IU/mL using the Rapid Fluorescent Focus Inhibition Test (RFFIT) assay. When administering HRIG: Calculate the dose in international units at 20 IU/kg based on the patient's body weight first and then convert the dose to milliliters using the concentration of the product on hand. Products made in the United States are available in different concentrations; verify the label before preparation and administration. Infiltrate HRIG into and around every identifiable wound to the extent that is anatomically feasible. Administer only the remaining volume in a different anatomic site from the first vaccine dose. If there is no identifiable wound, such as is common with a bat encounter, administer the entire HRIG dose intramuscularly at a site far from vaccine at a different anatomical site. Avoid gluteal administration of HRIG unless the wound is in the gluteal area. If HRIG was inadvertently administered in another anatomic site, additional HRIG may be administered to infiltrate the wound, as long as the total dose of HRIG administered to the patient doesn't exceed 40 IU/kg. Do not delay vaccination if HRIG is unavailable. HRIG can be administered until the patient’s third vaccine dose (day 7). HRIG administration is not recommended after three or more doses of vaccine have been given. Do not administer more than 40 IU/kg of HRIG, as higher doses might reduce vaccine-induced immunity. When the volume of HRIG is insufficient to cover all wounds, dilute with an appropriate diluent rather than increasing the total HRIG dose. Do not mix HRIG and vaccine in the same syringe or administer them in the same anatomical site. These products could neutralize each other, potentially making both ineffective. Do not give HRIG to a person who previously has completed PEP or a recognized pre-exposure prophylaxis course. 5. Administer rabies vaccine. For persons who were previously vaccinated against rabies, administer two doses of rabies vaccine on days 0 and 3. For persons who were never vaccinated against rabies, administer four doses of rabies vaccine at the time of the first medical visit (day 0), followed by an additional dose on days 3, 7, and 14 after the first dose, according to ACIP recommendations . Administer 1.0 mL of vaccine intramuscularly. Use the deltoid for adults and children older than 2 years; the anterolateral thigh is acceptable for children 2 years of age and younger. Do not administer rabies vaccine in the gluteal area. A dose given in the gluteal area is not considered valid and must be repeated at an appropriate site. 6. Determine if PEP is appropriate for people with compromised immune systems. If there is clinical suspicion that a patient’s medical history might negatively impact their ability to respond to vaccination (i.e., for patients who are immunocompromised), complete a five-dose vaccine series (days 0, 3, 7, 14, and 28) and confirm adequate vaccine response using serologic evidence via laboratory testing. Your health department can help coordinate expedited requests with the testing laboratory. CDC’s National Rabies Reference Laboratory can conduct serologic testing for U.S. patients who are immunocompromised or have evidence of failure to mount an adequate vaccine response. Contact the KDHE 24/7 Epidemiology Hotline to request serologic testing and discuss timing. CDC has recorded vaccination response failures among immunocompromised people who were exposed to rabies after completing a PEP series. These patients require additional consideration and immediate consultation with public health officials. 7. How to handle deviations in rabies post-exposure prophylaxis schedule. In general, deviations from the recommended vaccine schedule of up to several days are not of concern, but longer deviations require public health consultation. Use CDC's rabies PEP calculator to generate and evaluate rabies PEP schedules and to know when to consult a public health professional. 8. Contact the KDHE Epidemiology Hotline at 877-427-7317, option 5 or kdhe.epihotline@ks.gov for consultation for any situations where the need for administration of PEP is questionable or if there has been a significant deviation in PEP administration. Local Health Department Actions Requested 1. Provide timely consultation for rabies exposure risk assessments and PEP administration questions in your area. 2. Assist clinicians in evaluating rabies PEP administration errors before corrective biologics are given. Use CDC's rabies biologics guidance and CDC's rabies PEP calculator . 3. Monitor vaccine supplies and ensure processes are in place to procure from suppliers if allocation limits are implemented. 4. Share information on animal exposure and animal bite management with your community partners including veterinarians, animal shelters, and animal control agencies. Regulatory guidance can be found in the KDHE Rabies Control Requirements . Note that in Kansas, there is an option for animal PEP when unvaccinated animals are exposed or potentially exposed to rabies. Recommendations for the Public 1. Keep your distance from wildlife. Never approach animals who appear to be injured, sick, or dead, especially if you see animals during the day who are usually active at night (e.g., bats, raccoons, etc.). Contact your local animal control service for assistance when needed. Note that it is illegal to keep rabies reservoir species including raccoons, skunks, foxes, and coyotes as pets in Kansas. 2. If you have been in contact with any wildlife or sick-acting animals, particularly if you've been bitten or scratched, do the following: Wash any wounds immediately with water and soap (or water alone) for 15 minutes. Talk with a clinician or public health professional about your risk and if you might need rabies-related care. Tell your doctor about the type of animal you encountered and if you have noted any signs that the animal was not acting normally. If the animal that bit you was not your pet, ask the owner for proof that the animal is up to date on their rabies vaccination. If you can do so safely, capture or confine the animal and contact your local animal control service or your health department for assistance. In some circumstances and in consultation with a veterinarian, observing an available animal might be a reasonable alternative to rabies testing. 3. Bat encounters are a commonly reported wildlife exposure to rabies in Kansas. If you have direct contact with a bat or find a bat in your house, you may require additional healthcare to prevent rabies. Find more information on what to do following a bat encounter here: Bats, Rabies, and You . You can find out more about bats, the important role they play in our ecosystem, how to safely catch a bat should it enter your house, and how to prevent them from entering your home by reviewing our KDHE Bats in Kansas webpage . 4. If you have pets, keep them up to date on rabies vaccines and away from wildlife when possible. In some counties, rabies vaccination is required by law. 5. If your pet has been in contact with wildlife or involved in an animal bite situation, call your veterinarian to discuss appropriate wound care and rabies booster vaccination for your pet. For more information: KDHE has several resources that are available for clinicians, veterinarians, and local health departments to aid rabies risk assessment and appropriate post-exposure actions. For managing a potential human exposure to rabies, consult the risk assessment tool or printable flow chart for recommended actions. For animals that are exposed to rabies, follow the animal management flow chart . More information is available on the KDHE rabies webpage at https://www.kdhe.ks.gov/1497/Rabies . References: 1. news.content_original: News Flash Increase in Reported Human Rabies Exposures and Rabies Post-exposure Prophylaxis Administration Kansas Health Alert Network (KS-HAN) Posted on September 15, 2026 Summary The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Kansas Department of Health and Environment (KDHE) are issuing a Health Alert Network (HAN) Health Advisory in response to recent increases in encounters with potentially rabid animals, primarily bats in Kansas, and the associated need to perform a rabies risk assessment. Health departments and healthcare providers should be aware of the importance of rabies risk assessments before administering rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). Clinicians and healthcare facilities should ensure that rabies PEP is administered only when appropriate and that rabies vaccine and human rabies immune globulin (HRIG) is always administered according to ACIP recommendations. Background Rabies is a zoonotic viral disease that is nearly 100% fatal but is preventable when PEP is given appropriately before patient symptoms start. An infected animal can spread rabies to humans and other animals through bites, scratches, or oral secretions. Rabies primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to encephalitis and death if medical care is not received soon after exposure and before symptoms start. The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) post-exposure prophylaxis to prevent human rabies recommendations outline rabies exposure assessment, wound care, vaccination, and immunoglobulin dosing. Following a potential rabies exposure, it is important for a health official familiar with animal rabies epidemiology to help assess exposure risk and determine if a patient might need PEP. Two rabies vaccines, Imovax ® (HDCV) and RabAvert ® (PCECV), and two HRIG products, KEDRABTM and HyperRabTM , are licensed for use in people in the United States. Each year, an estimated 1.4 million people in the United States seek medical care after animal contact and undergo evaluation, and approximately 100,000 people receive rabies PEP following a potential exposure. According to weekly pharmacy data as of September 2, 2026, utilization for the two rabies vaccines and the two rabies immunoglobulins licensed in the United States has increased by an estimated 33% and 76%, respectively, compared with the same period last year. Although there is currently no shortage of human rabies vaccine or human rabies immunoglobulin in the United States, it is important for clinicians to administer PEP appropriately because errors in rabies risk assessment and PEP administration could result in unnecessary treatment (e.g., additional doses of vaccine or HRIG), potential adverse effects, and avoidable costs. A typical course of PEP can cost between $11,000 and $14,000 per person. Following rabies PEP administration guidance helps ensure that lifesaving vaccines are available for persons who need it and extraneous costs are avoided. Correct rabies PEP administration depends on the patient’s previous rabies vaccination status. For persons who have never been vaccinated against rabies, PEP should always include HRIG and vaccine. HRIG is administered once when PEP is initiated; if initially omitted, HRIG may be administered through the date of a patient’s third vaccination dose (day 7). HRIG is infiltrated into and around all identifiable wounds to the extent anatomically feasible, and any remaining volume is administered intramuscularly at a site distant from the first vaccine dose. Rabies vaccine is administered intramuscularly in the deltoid area (for adults) or in the deltoid or anterolateral thigh (for children) on days 0, 3, 7, and 14. Persons who were previously vaccinated against rabies should receive vaccine on days 0 and 3 and should not receive HRIG. Rabies vaccine is not administered in the gluteal area. HRIG and the first vaccine dose are never administered in the same syringe or anatomical site. Other recommendations apply to persons with altered immunity. Commonly reported errors in rabies PEP administration include: Administering rabies vaccine in the gluteal area. Failing to infiltrate HRIG into and around all identifiable wounds to the extent anatomically feasible. Administering HRIG and vaccine in the same syringe or anatomical site. Forgetting to give HRIG to someone who needs it. Administering HRIG to a person who was previously vaccinated against rabies. Misclassifying previous vaccination history or immune status, resulting in omitted or unnecessary biologics doses. Using an incorrect rabies vaccine schedule. Unnecessarily restarting the rabies vaccine series after a schedule deviation. Healthcare Provider Actions Requested 1. To encourage appropriate rabies PEP assessment and administration: Information on rabies epidemiology in Kansas and resources for clinicians are available on the KDHE rabies website . Contact your local health department or the 24/7 KDHE Epidemiology Hotline at 877-427-7317, option 5 for consultation on individual situations when needed. Be familiar with the complete CDC rabies post-exposure prophylaxis guidance. Learn common errors when administering rabies PEP and what to do to correct them. Ask patients about immunocompromising conditions, immunosuppressive medications, and prior rabies vaccination both in the United States and outside the country . Consult your hospital pharmacist if you have questions about rabies PEP administration for an individual patient. 2. Provide immediate wound care. Immediately and thoroughly wash each wound with water and soap (or water alone). If available, irrigate wounds with a virucidal agent such as povidone-iodine solution . Do not close the wound until HRIG has been administered. 3. Confirm that a rabies exposure occurred and that PEP is indicated. Promptly conduct a rabies risk assessment that considers the risk of rabies in the animal, the circumstances that led to the exposure, if the animal had any clinical signs consistent with rabies, and the type and severity of the wound. If needed, public health officials can help conduct the risk assessment. To help guide risk assessments, a CDC tool is available to help evaluate the risk of rabies in animals that are unable to undergo testing or observation periods. Verify prior rabies vaccination history to determine if the patient previously completed pre- or post-exposure prophylaxis. Check with your local public health authority to determine if suspect rabies exposures and animal bites are reportable. These are NOT reportable to KDHE. In general, PEP is not recommended when the animal is available for a 10-day post-exposure observation, rabies test results are negative, or health officials determine the exposure does not pose a rabies risk. 4. Administer HRIG only if the patient has not previously received rabies vaccine: A person is considered vaccinated for rabies if they have received either a full pre-exposure or post-exposure prophylaxis series OR a partial series followed by documentation of a serologic titer ≥0.5 IU/mL using the Rapid Fluorescent Focus Inhibition Test (RFFIT) assay. When administering HRIG: Calculate the dose in international units at 20 IU/kg based on the patient's body weight first and then convert the dose to milliliters using the concentration of the product on hand. Products made in the United States are available in different concentrations; verify the label before preparation and administration. Infiltrate HRIG into and around every identifiable wound to the extent that is anatomically feasible. Administer only the remaining volume in a different anatomic site from the first vaccine dose. If there is no identifiable wound, such as is common with a bat encounter, administer the entire HRIG dose intramuscularly at a site far from vaccine at a different anatomical site. Avoid gluteal administration of HRIG unless the wound is in the gluteal area. If HRIG was inadvertently administered in another anatomic site, additional HRIG may be administered to infiltrate the wound, as long as the total dose of HRIG administered to the patient doesn't exceed 40 IU/kg. Do not delay vaccination if HRIG is unavailable. HRIG can be administered until the patient’s third vaccine dose (day 7). HRIG administration is not recommended after three or more doses of vaccine have been given. Do not administer more than 40 IU/kg of HRIG, as higher doses might reduce vaccine-induced immunity. When the volume of HRIG is insufficient to cover all wounds, dilute with an appropriate diluent rather than increasing the total HRIG dose. Do not mix HRIG and vaccine in the same syringe or administer them in the same anatomical site. These products could neutralize each other, potentially making both ineffective. Do not give HRIG to a person who previously has completed PEP or a recognized pre-exposure prophylaxis course. 5. Administer rabies vaccine. For persons who were previously vaccinated against rabies, administer two doses of rabies vaccine on days 0 and 3. For persons who were never vaccinated against rabies, administer four doses of rabies vaccine at the time of the first medical visit (day 0), followed by an additional dose on days 3, 7, and 14 after the first dose, according to ACIP recommendations . Administer 1.0 mL of vaccine intramuscularly. Use the deltoid for adults and children older than 2 years; the anterolateral thigh is acceptable for children 2 years of age and younger. Do not administer rabies vaccine in the gluteal area. A dose given in the gluteal area is not considered valid and must be repeated at an appropriate site. 6. Determine if PEP is appropriate for people with compromised immune systems. If there is clinical suspicion that a patient’s medical history might negatively impact their ability to respond to vaccination (i.e., for patients who are immunocompromised), complete a five-dose vaccine series (days 0, 3, 7, 14, and 28) and confirm adequate vaccine response using serologic evidence via laboratory testing. Your health department can help coordinate expedited requests with the testing laboratory. CDC’s National Rabies Reference Laboratory can conduct serologic testing for U.S. patients who are immunocompromised or have evidence of failure to mount an adequate vaccine response. Contact the KDHE 24/7 Epidemiology Hotline to request serologic testing and discuss timing. CDC has recorded vaccination response failures among immunocompromised people who were exposed to rabies after completing a PEP series. These patients require additional consideration and immediate consultation with public health officials. 7. How to handle deviations in rabies post-exposure prophylaxis schedule. In general, deviations from the recommended vaccine schedule of up to several days are not of concern, but longer deviations require public health consultation. Use CDC's rabies PEP calculator to generate and evaluate rabies PEP schedules and to know when to consult a public health professional. 8. Contact the KDHE Epidemiology Hotline at 877-427-7317, option 5 or kdhe.epihotline@ks.gov for consultation for any situations where the need for administration of PEP is questionable or if there has been a significant deviation in PEP administration. Local Health Department Actions Requested 1. Provide timely consultation for rabies exposure risk assessments and PEP administration questions in your area. 2. Assist clinicians in evaluating rabies PEP administration errors before corrective biologics are given. Use CDC's rabies biologics guidance and CDC's rabies PEP calculator . 3. Monitor vaccine supplies and ensure processes are in place to procure from suppliers if allocation limits are implemented. 4. Share information on animal exposure and animal bite management with your community partners including veterinarians, animal shelters, and animal control agencies. Regulatory guidance can be found in the KDHE Rabies Control Requirements . Note that in Kansas, there is an option for animal PEP when unvaccinated animals are exposed or potentially exposed to rabies. Recommendations for the Public 1. Keep your distance from wildlife. Never approach animals who appear to be injured, sick, or dead, especially if you see animals during the day who are usually active at night (e.g., bats, raccoons, etc.). Contact your local animal control service for assistance when needed. Note that it is illegal to keep rabies reservoir species including raccoons, skunks, foxes, and coyotes as pets in Kansas. 2. If you have been in contact with any wildlife or sick-acting animals, particularly if you've been bitten or scratched, do the following: Wash any wounds immediately with water and soap (or water alone) for 15 minutes. Talk with a clinician or public health professional about your risk and if you might need rabies-related care. Tell your doctor about the type of animal you encountered and if you have noted any signs that the animal was not acting normally. If the animal that bit you was not your pet, ask the owner for proof that the animal is up to date on their rabies vaccination. If you can do so safely, capture or confine the animal and contact your local animal control service or your health department for assistance. In some circumstances and in consultation with a veterinarian, observing an available animal might be a reasonable alternative to rabies testing. 3. Bat encounters are a commonly reported wildlife exposure to rabies in Kansas. If you have direct contact with a bat or find a bat in your house, you may require additional healthcare to prevent rabies. Find more information on what to do following a bat encounter here: Bats, Rabies, and You . You can find out more about bats, the important role they play in our ecosystem, how to safely catch a bat should it enter your house, and how to prevent them from entering your home by reviewing our KDHE Bats in Kansas webpage . 4. If you have pets, keep them up to date on rabies vaccines and away from wildlife when possible. In some counties, rabies vaccination is required by law. 5. If your pet has been in contact with wildlife or involved in an animal bite situation, call your veterinarian to discuss appropriate wound care and rabies booster vaccination for your pet. For more information: KDHE has several resources that are available for clinicians, veterinarians, and local health departments to aid rabies risk assessment and appropriate post-exposure actions. For managing a potential human exposure to rabies, consult the risk assessment tool or printable flow chart for recommended actions. For animals that are exposed to rabies, follow the animal management flow chart . More information is available on the KDHE rabies webpage at https://www.kdhe.ks.gov/1497/Rabies . References: 1. news.source_body_en: The Kansas Department of Health and Environment (KDHE) has issued a Health Alert Network Health Advisory due to an increase in reported human rabies exposures and rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) administration in Kansas. Rabies PEP utilization has increased by 33% and 76% for vaccines and immunoglobulins, respectively, compared to the same period last year. Common errors in PEP administration include incorrect vaccine schedules, improper HRIG administration, and misclassifying previous vaccination history. Healthcare providers are advised to consult KDHE resources for guidance on appropriate PEP administration.
news.content_zh: 由于堪萨斯州报告的人类 狂犬病 暴露和 狂犬病 暴露后预防 (PEP) 管理的增加,堪萨斯州健康与环境部 (KDHE) 发布了健康警报网络健康咨询。与去年同期相比,狂犬病 疫苗 和免疫球蛋白的 PEP 利用率分别增加了 33% 和 76%。PEP 管理中的常见错误包括不正确的 疫苗 计划、不正确的 HRIG 管理以及错误分类以前的 疫苗接种 历史记录。建议医疗保健提供者查阅 KDHE 资源,获取有关适当 PEP 管理的指导。
news.summary_zh: 由于堪萨斯州报告的人类 狂犬病 暴露和 狂犬病 暴露后预防 (PEP) 管理的增加,堪萨斯州健康与环境部 (KDHE) 发布了健康警报网络健康咨询。与去年同期相比,狂犬病 疫苗 和免疫球蛋白的 PEP 利用率分别增加了 33% 和 76%。PEP 管理中的常见错误包括不正确的 疫苗 计划、不正确的 HRIG 管理以及错误分类以前的 疫苗接种 历史记录。建议医疗保健提供者查阅 KDHE 资源,获取有关适当 PEP 管理的指导。

is possible A decade of political commitment, community action and One Health collaboration brings Bhutan a historic milestone 16 September 2026 Reading time: The World Health Organization (WHO) has validated Bhutan as having eliminated dog-mediated human rabies as a public health problem — the first country in the WHO South-East Asia Region and one of only three countries in the world, with Chile and Mexico, to achieve this milestone. Bhutan has recorded zero human deaths from dog-mediated rabies since June 2023. For families across Bhutan, this means no longer living with the fear of a fatal dog bite — a threat long familiar to rural communities.The validation, announced ahead of World Rabies Day on 28 September, follows more than a decade of steadyand strategic investments by the Royal Government of Bhutan under the visionary and benevolent leadership of His Majesty The King — and offers a real example for other countries chasing the same goal: "Zero by 30," ending human deaths from dog-mediated rabies worldwide by 2030. Bhutan's success didn't come from one sector working alone The turning point came in 2021, when a Royal Decree by His Majesty The King brought veterinarians, De-suung, health workers and communities together under a "One Health" approach, launching the Nationwide Accelerated Dog Population Management and Rabies Control Programme (NADPM&RCP). The programme was spearheaded by the Department of Livestock in partnership with De-suung. His Majesty’s initiative provided a significant impetus to advancing Bhutan’s 2019 pledge towards the global Zero by 30 goal. “For years, this has been a shared national endeavour, driven by the leadership of His Majesty The King, dedication of our veterinary and health professionals, De-suung volunteers, local governments and communities. Bhutan’s achievement belongs to every one of them. This milestone is not the end, we remain committed to staying vigilant and sustaining our efforts so that no family in Bhutan ever has to fear losing a loved one to rabies again” said the Minister of Health, Ministry of Health, Royal Government of Bhutan. The programme and communities in action: villagers bring their dogs to a registration point during the nationwide NADPM&RCP campaign. Credit: National Accelerated Dog Population Management and Rabies Control Programme, Bhutan. Making sure treatment was always within reach At the heart of the programme was a commitment that no one in Bhutan would be turned away from treatment. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) — the wound care, vaccination and, when needed, immunoglobulin that prevents rabies after a bite or scratch — has remained accessible and free of charge across all 20 Dzongkhags (districts), sustained through dedicated financing from the Bhutan Health Trust Fund. Alongside this, Bhutan strengthened surveillance across human and animal health so that any suspected case could be picked up and investigated without delay. The programme also protected the people delivering it: every De-suung volunteer and livestock worker involved in fieldwork received pre-exposure rabies vaccination before deployment. A De-suung volunteer receives intradermal pre-exposure rabies vaccination before joining fieldwork. Credit: National Accelerated Dog Population Management and Rabies Control Programme, Bhutan. Reaching every corner of the country, together To break the chain of transmission, Bhutan ran an intensified nationwide campaign that vaccinated more than 90% of the free-roaming dog population — well above the 70% coverage WHO recommends to interrupt the disease's spread. None of this would have been possible without Bhutan's De-suung (Guardians of Peace) national volunteers, who carried the programme into every corner of the country — often across difficult terrain — from dog census work to public awareness. Local communities played their part too: bringing dogs forward for sterilisation, reporting sightings, and supporting field teams. Dog population management ran alongside vaccination — large-scale sterilisation, pet microchipping and registration, and responsible pet ownership education — culminating in 100% sterilisation coverage of the free-roaming dog population. De-suung volunteers record data and issue dog vaccination cards to the community at a mobile registration desk during the nationwide NADPM&RCP campaign. Credit: National Accelerated Dog Population Management and Rabies Control Programme, Bhutan. How the achievement was verified The achievement follows a rigorous, independent validation process — a desk review of Bhutan's technical dossier, followed by a field mission across the country in August 2026. It confirms not just Bhutan's past success, but the systems now in place to prevent rabies from re-emerging. Sustaining the gains, and looking ahead Bhutan's work does not stop with validation — vaccination, population management and surveillance will continue, with closer coordination with neighbouring endemic states to guard against rabies crossing back over the border. Bhutan's story shows that ending human deaths from dog-mediated rabies is possible — even across mountainous terrain and busy borders — when political will, free treatment, sustained vaccination and community ownership move together. As the world marks World Rabies Day on 28 September under this year's theme, 'Stronger Together,' Bhutan stands as proof of what that looks like in practice: a path other countries can follow to Zero by 30. Children gather with their dogs during the nationwide NADPM&RCP campaign. Credit: National Accelerated Dog Population Management and Rabies Control Programme, Bhutan. Colombo, Sep. 16 (Daily Mirror) - The proposed Rabies Eradication and Dog Registration Bill could potentially disrupt Sri Lanka’s dog vaccination programme and increase the risk of human rabies, the Sri Lanka Public Health Inspectors Association (SLPHIA) has warned. In a letter to President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, the association urged the Government to review the Bill, saying several of its provisions could create practical difficulties in maintaining the country’s existing community-based rabies control programme. Sri Lanka’s Ministry of Health has identified dog vaccination as a key component of its rabies prevention strategy. The country’s National Strategic Plan targets dog vaccination coverage of more than 75 per cent and zero dog-mediated human rabies deaths by 2026. The association said Sri Lanka’s dog rabies vaccination programme had a long history, dating back to 1953, and was currently implemented through the Ministry of Health’s Public Health Veterinary Service, District Rabies Control Units and Medical Officer of Health (MOH) areas. Public Health Inspectors (PHIs), it said, play a key role in taking vaccination services to communities, including vaccination of domestic dogs, stray dogs and dogs found around schools, temples, public places and government and private institutions. The association also said special vaccination programmes were conducted in areas where dog bites or suspected rabies cases were reported, based on surveillance carried out at the location. According to the PHIs, the proposed legislation could create a major obstacle to this system. The association specifically raised concerns over Section 4 of the Bill, which it said would require dog vaccination to be carried out by a veterinarian or under a veterinarian’s supervision. It claimed that there are currently no veterinarians attached to MOH-level health services to conduct the existing vaccination programme, while only a limited number of the country’s 341 local authorities have veterinarians attached to them. The association therefore warned that the existing vaccination activities could be forced to stop once the proposed law comes into effect unless an alternative mechanism is established. The PHIs said this was particularly concerning given the link between sustained dog vaccination and the long-term reduction in human rabies deaths in Sri Lanka. According to the Ministry of Health, 20 laboratory-confirmed human rabies deaths were reported in 2024, while dogs remained the main reservoir and primary source responsible for most human rabies deaths that year. The World Health Organization has also identified dog vaccination and post-exposure prophylaxis as key public health interventions behind Sri Lanka’s substantial reduction in human rabies deaths, from 377 deaths in the mid-1970s to 31 in 2021. The association further referred to a change made in 2018, when responsibility for dog vaccination was transferred to veterinarians of the Department of Animal Production and Health and District Rabies Control Units under the Health Ministry were discontinued. It claimed that only about six per cent of dogs were vaccinated under that arrangement in 2018 and that the programme was subsequently returned to the Health Ministry in 2019. The association said District Rabies Control Units were then reactivated and vaccination activities resumed, with the Health Ministry working towards reducing human rabies deaths and ultimately eliminating dog-mediated human rabies. The PHIs also raised concerns over the proposed Bill’s enforcement mechanism. It said the draft identifies Medical Officers of Health and police officers as authorised officers but does not include Public Health Inspectors, despite PHIs being directly involved in community-level health activities and frequently receiving complaints about dog bites, suspected rabies cases and problems associated with dog ownership. The association argued that excluding PHIs could create difficulties in enforcing the proposed law at grassroots level and responding to complaints from the public. It also questioned the practicality of requiring Medical Officers of Health to undertake all field-level activities, claiming that powers vested in an MOH under the proposed legislation could not be delegated to a PHI or another officer. The proposed legislation is intended to consolidate Sri Lanka’s existing Rabies Ordinance and Dog Registration Ordinance, make rabies vaccination of dogs mandatory, strengthen dog population control and clarify the responsibilities of institutions involved in rabies control and dog registration. Cabinet approved its publication in the Gazette before submission to Parliament. The association said it supported efforts to eradicate rabies but urged the Government to amend the proposed legislation to ensure that the law is practical at grassroots level and does not disrupt the existing vaccination system. It requested President Dissanayake to review the Bill and introduce the necessary amendments before it is implemented. Colombo, Sep. 16 (Daily Mirror) - The proposed Rabies Eradication and Dog Registration Bill could potentially disrupt Sri Lanka’s dog vaccination programme and increase the risk of human rabies, the Sri Lanka Public Health Inspectors Association (SLPHIA) has warned. In a letter to President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, the association urged the Government to review the Bill, saying several of its provisions could create practical difficulties in maintaining the country’s existing community-based rabies control programme. Sri Lanka’s Ministry of Health has identified dog vaccination as a key component of its rabies prevention strategy. The country’s National Strategic Plan targets dog vaccination coverage of more than 75 per cent and zero dog-mediated human rabies deaths by 2026. The association said Sri Lanka’s dog rabies vaccination programme had a long history, dating back to 1953, and was currently implemented through the Ministry of Health’s Public Health Veterinary Service, District Rabies Control Units and Medical Officer of Health (MOH) areas. Public Health Inspectors (PHIs), it said, play a key role in taking vaccination services to communities, including vaccination of domestic dogs, stray dogs and dogs found around schools, temples, public places and government and private institutions. The association also said special vaccination programmes were conducted in areas where dog bites or suspected rabies cases were reported, based on surveillance carried out at the location. According to the PHIs, the proposed legislation could create a major obstacle to this system. The association specifically raised concerns over Section 4 of the Bill, which it said would require dog vaccination to be carried out by a veterinarian or under a veterinarian’s supervision. It claimed that there are currently no veterinarians attached to MOH-level health services to conduct the existing vaccination programme, while only a limited number of the country’s 341 local authorities have veterinarians attached to them. The association therefore warned that the existing vaccination activities could be forced to stop once the proposed law comes into effect unless an alternative mechanism is established. The PHIs said this was particularly concerning given the link between sustained dog vaccination and the long-term reduction in human rabies deaths in Sri Lanka. According to the Ministry of Health, 20 laboratory-confirmed human rabies deaths were reported in 2024, while dogs remained the main reservoir and primary source responsible for most human rabies deaths that year. The World Health Organization has also identified dog vaccination and post-exposure prophylaxis as key public health interventions behind Sri Lanka’s substantial reduction in human rabies deaths, from 377 deaths in the mid-1970s to 31 in 2021. The association further referred to a change made in 2018, when responsibility for dog vaccination was transferred to veterinarians of the Department of Animal Production and Health and District Rabies Control Units under the Health Ministry were discontinued. It claimed that only about six per cent of dogs were vaccinated under that arrangement in 2018 and that the programme was subsequently returned to the Health Ministry in 2019. The association said District Rabies Control Units were then reactivated and vaccination activities resumed, with the Health Ministry working towards reducing human rabies deaths and ultimately eliminating dog-mediated human rabies. The PHIs also raised concerns over the proposed Bill’s enforcement mechanism. It said the draft identifies Medical Officers of Health and police officers as authorised officers but does not include Public Health Inspectors, despite PHIs being directly involved in community-level health activities and frequently receiving complaints about dog bites, suspected rabies cases and problems associated with dog ownership. The association argued that excluding PHIs could create difficulties in enforcing the proposed law at grassroots level and responding to complaints from the public. It also questioned the practicality of requiring Medical Officers of Health to undertake all field-level activities, claiming that powers vested in an MOH under the proposed legislation could not be delegated to a PHI or another officer. The proposed legislation is intended to consolidate Sri Lanka’s existing Rabies Ordinance and Dog Registration Ordinance, make rabies vaccination of dogs mandatory, strengthen dog population control and clarify the responsibilities of institutions involved in rabies control and dog registration. Cabinet approved its publication in the Gazette before submission to Parliament. The association said it supported efforts to eradicate rabies but urged the Government to amend the proposed legislation to ensure that the law is practical at grassroots level and does not disrupt the existing vaccination system. It requested President Dissanayake to review the Bill and introduce the necessary amendments before it is implemented. news.content_zh: 斯里兰卡拟议的《狂犬病 根除和狗登记法案》引起了公共卫生监察员协会 (PHIA) 的担忧,该协会警告说,该立法可能会扰乱该国的狗 狂犬病 活动,并增加人类 狂犬病 的风险。该法案正在接受政府审查,要求狗 疫苗接种 必须由兽医进行或在兽医的监督下进行。然而,当前的 疫苗接种 计划依赖公共卫生检查员 (PHI) 和卫生官员 (MOH) 来接触社区,包括流浪狗和家养狗。PHIA 认为,卫生部级别的服务中缺乏兽医以及将 PHI 排除在执法之外可能会阻碍该计划的有效性。卫生部指出,狗是 狂犬病 的主要 狂犬病,也是大多数人类 狂犬病 死亡的原因,2024 年报告了 20 起实验室确诊病例。该协会支持根除 狂犬病,但敦促进行修订,以确保该法案切实可行,不会破坏现有的努力。世界卫生组织已将狗 疫苗接种 和 暴露后预防 视为减少人类 狂犬病 死亡人数的关键干预措施,多年来人类死亡人数已大幅下降。该法案的实施仍存在不确定性,呼吁在其成为法律之前进行审查和调整。

news.title_original: Feds fight rabies amid concerning rise in animal cases, human exposures - CIDRAP

analysis.time: ‘It’s a huge concern’: Families of kids with complex medical needs worry about frequent measles outbreaks Meghan Holohan For children with complex medical conditions, infection with the highly contagious virus could lead to a hospital stay.
analysis.event: Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) is addressing a concerning rise in rabies cases among animals and human exposures, with a focus on rabies-infected animals leading to vaccine series for individuals.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The event involves 177 additional cases reported by the CDC, with 767 cases in Pennsylvania alone. There is a risk of rabies transmission to humans, particularly to children with complex medical conditions.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The HHS is taking action, including issuing a request for vaccine series for individuals exposed to rabies-infected animals. The status is under investigation and communication with the public is ongoing.

analysis.brief_en: The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services is addressing a concerning rise in rabies cases among animals and human exposures, particularly in Minnesota and Pennsylvania. With 767 cases in Pennsylvania alone, there is a risk of rabies transmission to humans, especially to children with complex medical conditions. The HHS is issuing vaccine series for exposed individuals and is under investigation, with ongoing public communication.
analysis.summary_en: The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services is addressing a concerning rise in rabies cases among animals and human exposures, particularly in Minnesota and Pennsylvania. With 767 cases in Pennsylvania alone, there is a risk of rabies transmission to humans, especially to children with complex medical conditions. The HHS is issuing vaccine series for exposed individuals and is under investigation, with ongoing public communication.

news.title: 2 bats in Pueblo County test positive for rabies. Here’s what to know
news.excerpt: Two rabid bats were recently found in separate locations in Pueblo County. Here's what to know about the disease, its dangers, and what to look for.

news.content_title: 2 bats test positive for rabies in Pueblo County, what to know
news.content: Two rabid bats were recently found in separate locations in Pueblo County, and the Pueblo Department of Public Health and Environment is urging people to stay away from wildlife and vaccinate their pets for rabies . Rabies is a viral disease that is deadly if people don't receive medical care before symptoms start. The disease spreads primarily through bites or scratches from an infected animal. According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention , rabies attacks the nervous system and is nearly always fatal once symptoms appear. The animals most frequently found with rabies in the U.S. are bats, skunks, raccoons, and foxes. "Rabies is caused by a virus transmitted by the bite of an infected animal," Scott Cowan, PDPHE program manager, said in a news release. "Rabies also can be transmitted if the infected animal's saliva gets into a cut or break in the skin or through the eyes, nose, or mouth. Without proper medical intervention for humans or preventative vaccination for domestic animals, rabies is fatal." If a bat is found inside of a home or comes into contact with humans or pets, it should be tested for rabies. "A bat's teeth are very small and sharp; a bite wound may not be visible," PDPHE officials said in the release. "If a bat is found, immediately leave the area and take your pets away from the bat. news.content: Skip to Main Content Skip to audio player to listen live Stay Curious. Stay Connected. Newsletters♡Donate Now Menu Search Sign in Menu Programs & Podcasts Schedule Ways to Give Search Sign in Health Hannah Yang Mankato, Minn. September 17, 2026 6:05 PM Rabies confirmed in Brown County cow. MDH recommends shots for 9 people who were exposed A Brown County cow was confirmed to have rabies, according to the Minnesota Board of Animal Health. The heifer was euthanized and the head was removed for rabies testing at the Minnesota Department of Health Public Health Laboratory. Brain tissue tested positive for the rabies virus on Sept. 8. Dan Gunderson | MPR News file ListenRabies confirmed in Brown County cow. MDH recommends shots for 9 people who were exposed Go Deeper. Create an account or log in to save stories. Log in Like this? Thanks for liking this story! We have added it to a list of your favorite stories. Show me! Save Share The Minnesota Board of Animal Health confirmed that a cow in Brown County tested positive for rabies last week after it was euthanized. The board said the owner of the heifer noticed the animal behaving oddly on Sept. 1 as it laid flat with its head down. A veterinarian observed the animal the same day and the owner had administered oral medication with bare hands. Another veterinarian examined the animal the following day and also gave it oral medication without wearing gloves. A third veterinarian examined the animal on Sept. 3 and observed that the cow had uncoordinated hind legs and was high-stepping, vocalizing, hypersalivating and had a high temperature. The heifer was euthanized and the head was removed for rabies testing at the Minnesota Department of Health Public Health Laboratory. Brain tissue tested positive for the rabies virus on Sept. 8. Turn Up Your Support MPR News helps you turn down the noise and build shared understanding. Turn up your support for this public resource and keep trusted journalism accessible to all. Public health officials recommended that nine people who came in contact with the animal and its saliva, including the owner of the dairy cow, the owner’s daughter, two minor children, two of the veterinarians who examined the animal and three assisting veterinary technicians seek rabies post-exposure prophylaxis as a preventative measure. Experts say the disease is extremely dangerous and life-threatening to both humans and animals. “A lot of times, it eventually travels up to the brain and will cause encephalopathy and eventually lead to death,” said Dr. Katie Cornille, senior veterinarian at the state Board of Animal Health. “It is a fatal disease, so it’s something that we take very seriously.” The Board quarantined 13 other cows on the same Brown County farm so they can be monitored for rabies symptoms. More than 40 cattle on the property will also be watched for any signs of rabies symptoms. A horse on the property was also possibly exposed, but it is up-to-date on its rabies vaccinations, along with three vaccinated dogs. They are all under observation as well, while two unvaccinated barn cats that were likely exposed to rabies were euthanized. Once a domestic animal is exposed, it can take anywhere from two to 26 weeks for symptoms of rabies to develop, depending on the location of the bite and the amount of the virus that enters the body. Most domestic animals that show symptoms will die within three to 12 weeks. To help prevent spreading the virus and to reduce exposure to other animals, the Minnesota Board of Animal Health places all domestic animals that have been exposed and are unvaccinated under a 45- to 180-day quarantine. “Every case of rabies is going to be serious,” Cornille said. “I’m sure the individuals that own the animals, they’re handling the loss of the animal, and they don’t want to lose anymore. We want to make sure that if there are any infectious animals that they don’t spread it anywhere else.” In Minnesota, skunks and bats are the most common carriers of the rabies virus. Dan Gunderson | MPR News file Rabies is most often spread by being bitten by a rabid animal, and health officials say the cow was likely bitten by a rabid skunk or bat. Skunks and bats are the most common natural carriers of rabies in Minnesota. Multiple skunks were observed earlier this year on a neighboring plot of land that connected to the area where the rabid cow was held. Wild animals account for the vast majority of rabies cases reported annually in the state, and fewer than 15 percent of cases reported each year are in domesticated species. The most common domestic animals infected by rabies are cattle, cats and dogs — and the symptoms each animal may show can vary. Rabies prevention Rabies is a preventable viral disease that affects the central nervous system in mammals and causes encephalopathy and eventually death. It’s most commonly transmitted through the bite of a rabid animal, but can also be spread through saliva. However, once a person displays symptoms it’s already too late to receive treatment, said Dr. Carrie Klumb, senior epidemiologist at MDH. “With rabies, once you’re showing symptoms, there’s no treatment that’s been shown to actually work and keep people alive,” Klumb said. “What we have to do is that if you’ve had an exposure to the virus, we need to give you the rabies vaccination before you ever show any symptoms, so that you never show any symptoms and you never develop the disease.” The situation in Brown County, Klumb said, highlights the need for biosecurity and also prevention, and she urges those caring for farm animals “to take appropriate steps to put your personal protective equipment on before you treat the animal.” Since bats are also rabies carriers, only researchers with appropriate vaccinations are allowed to handle them. Wearing two pairs of gloves helps but is no guarantee in Itasca State Park on June 15. Monika Lawrence for MPR News file “If you do have an ill animal that you’re caring for, remembering those basic things like: cover your eyes, nose and mouth,” Klum added. “Put some gloves on, call your veterinarian, make sure a professional can come evaluate your animal, or bring your animal into the vet to be evaluated.” Although the case in Brown County focused on a cow, for Minnesotans Klumb said it’s more likely there will be encounters with a bat. About one percent of bats in the wild are believed to be carrying rabies. About three to four percent of bats MDH tests each year test positive for rabies. Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search CLOSE Search Support Menu Feds fight rabies amid concerning rise in animal cases, human exposures Mary Van Beusekom, MS Rabies Natasa_M / iStock Share Copied to clipboard As the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) warns of a nationwide increase in animal rabies cases and human exposures, the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) has announced it is about to conduct its annual airdrop of millions of fishmeal-coated sachets of rabies vaccine over the Southeast to immunize wildlife against the deadly disease. Last week, the CDC issued a Health Alert Network advisory after observing a 17% increase in questions about human exposures to rabid or possibly rabid animals in July and August over the same period in 2025. “During this time frame, CDC also received reports from at least eight state health departments of increased rabies PEP [post-exposure prophylaxis] use, PEP administration errors, or both,” the CDC said. PEP consists of administration of two human rabies immunoglobulin (antibody) doses and a four-dose vaccine series. Each course costs up to $14,000. “According to weekly pharmacy data as of September 2, 2026, utilization for the two rabies vaccines and the two rabies immunoglobulins licensed in the United States has increased by an estimated 33% and 76%, respectively, compared with the same time period last year,” it added. As of September 2, 2026, utilization for the two rabies vaccines and the two rabies immunoglobulins licensed in the United States has increased by an estimated 33% and 76%, respectively, compared with the same time period last year. As part of an ongoing program, the USDA is distributing oral rabies vaccine sachets via airplane, helicopter, and motor vehicle over parts of Alabama, Georgia, North Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia, and West Virginia in October to counter the spread of raccoon rabies. Raccoons are the main rabies transmitter in the region. Each year, the USDA distributes about 6.5 million vaccine sachets in targeted areas. The distribution has been successful in targeting canine rabies in coyotes and a variant of the disease in gray foxes. Officials said they plan to move the raccoon vaccine distribution area east as rabies is eliminated locally and regionally. The case for proper protection Each year from 2016 to 2025, Minnesota tests more than 21,000 animals for rabies, with only small fractions testing positive, except for skunks, about half of which either test positive or are untestable. Yesterday, the Minnesota Board of Animal Health confirmed that a cow in Brown County tested positive for rabies last week, leading to the quarantine of 13 cows and PEP recommendations for nine people. The heifer’s owner noticed the cow lying flat with its head down, the board said in a news release. After a vet visited that same day, the owner gave the animal oral medication with bare hands. The next day, another vet visited and also administered the oral drug without wearing gloves. A day later, a third vet euthanized the cow after observing that the animal had uncoordinated hind legs and a high fever and was high-stepping, vocalizing, and salivating excessively. Less than 15% of rabid animal cases reported annually in Minnesota occur in domestic species; the most common being cattle, cats, and dogs. In addition to the quarantine of 13 cows, two unvaccinated barn cats with likely exposure were euthanized, and more than 40 cattle, a vaccinated horse, and three unvaccinated dogs are under observation. “Less than 15% of rabid animal cases reported annually in Minnesota occur in domestic species; the most common being cattle, cats, and dogs,” the release said, noting that rabies vaccines are available for cats, dogs, ferrets, cattle, horses, and sheep. “Skunks and bats are the natural carriers of rabies in Minnesota.” Given the severity of rabies, the board urged the use of personal protective equipment such as gloves and eye protection when interacting with animals that could have rabies. An unusual request from health officials In an unrelated case, last week, the Minnesota Department of Health (MDH) asked customers of ASAP Wildlife Services MN who had bats or other mammals submitted for rabies testing since September 2025 to let them know. “Officials believe ASAP Wildlife Services MN operates in the Twin Cities metro area and has not consistently submitted animals for rabies testing,” the MDH said in a news release. “At least one customer has been told of negative results from a laboratory that does not perform animal rabies testing.” The company has not responded to MDH requests for information. Each year in the United States, roughly 1.4 million people seek medical care after animal contact and undergo rabies evaluation, and about 100,000 receive rabies PEP, the CDC said. elements_zh.time: CDC上周发布健康警报网络咨询,截至2026年9月2日,狂犬病、疫苗和免疫球蛋白的使用量与去年同期相比分别增加了33%和76%。美国农业部计划在 10 月份分发 疫苗,明尼苏达州动物健康委员会上周证实一头牛的 狂犬病 检测呈阳性。
elements_zh.location_and_population: 这些事件在美国都有报道,特别是在美国农业部空投的东南地区和明尼苏达州的牛 狂犬病 病例中。受影响的人群包括野生动物、家畜和接触过患有狂犬病的动物的人类。
elements_zh.event: 美国疾病控制和预防中心 (CDC) 报告称,与 2025 年同期相比,2026 年 7 月和 8 月有关人类接触患有狂犬病或可能患有狂犬病的动物的问题增加了 17%。美国农业部每年都会在东南部空投 狂犬病 疫苗,为野生动物提供免疫接种。明尼苏达州布朗县的一头奶牛 狂犬病 检测呈阳性,因此提出了隔离和 PEP 建议。
elements_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: CDC 收到至少八个州卫生部门的报告,称 狂犬病 PEP 使用量增加、管理错误或两者兼而有之。在明尼苏达州,不到 15% 的狂犬病动物病例发生在家养动物中,其中牛、猫和狗是最常见的。超过 40 头牛、一匹接种疫苗的马和三只未接种疫苗的狗正在接受观察。每门 PEP 课程的费用高达 14,000 美元。
elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 美国农业部将于 10 月份通过飞机、直升机和机动车辆在目标地区分发口服 狂犬病 疫苗 小袋。明尼苏达州动物健康委员会确认了这头牛的病例,并敦促在与可能感染 狂犬病 的动物互动时使用个人防护装备。CDC 正在监测情况,尚未确认任何 2026 年 狂犬病 死亡病例。

Check out the Fetch On-Demand Catalog| Veterinary Podcast Advertisement News|Articles|September 15, 2026 Amid new CDC advisory, AVMA details recent rabies exposure incidents, reiterates vaccination policy Author(s)Justin Louis, Content Producer Fact checked by: Yasmeen Qahwash Several rabies exposure incidents have been reported across multiple states, days after the CDC issued a health advisory on rising human rabies exposures and errors in postexposure prophylaxis administration. Advertisement The American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA) detailed several recent rabies exposure incidents involving a variety of animal species and reiterated its existing rabies policy, following a September 10 Health Alert Network advisory from the CDC on a nationwide increase in reported human rabies exposures and errors in rabies postexposure prophylaxis (PEP) administration.1,2 From July through August 2026, the CDC received 17% more rabies-related inquiries than during the same period in 2025, and local health departments reported increases in human rabies exposures, including from animals in which rabies is uncommon. At least 8 state health departments reported increased rabies PEP use, PEP administration errors, or both over the past 3 months.2 RELATED: CDC reports increase in rabies exposures and PEP use in multiple US jurisdictions Advertisement AVMA News highlighted several such incidents. In North Carolina, health officials investigated an outbreak linked to a traveling petting zoo where visitors were exposed to rabies-positive baby goats; more than 260 people were subsequently advised to receive PEP as a result. Other cases identified since July include 2 rabid-beaver attacks at a Maryland state park, a New Jersey man bitten on the leg by a rabid raccoon, and an incident in New Hampshire in which an animal believed to be either a gray fox or a fisher attacked 3 people.1 As of September 2, use of the 2 rabies vaccines and 2 human rabies immune globulin products licensed in the United States had increased by an estimated 33% and 76%, respectively, compared with the same period last year.2 AVMA News noted that a typical PEP course can cost up to $14,000 per person.1 Annually, an estimated 1.4 million people in the US seek medical care after suspected contact with a rabid animal, and approximately 100,000 receive PEP.2 Fewer than 10 human rabies deaths are reported in the US each year, and in 2024, there were 3834 reported cases of rabies among animals nationwide, according to AVMA News.1 AVMA policy underscores vaccination AVMA News reiterated the association's existing policy on rabies, which states, in part: "Rabies is an almost invariably fatal disease for animals and humans. AVMA endorses the 2016 Compendium of Animal Rabies Prevention and Control, developed by the National Association of State Public Health Veterinarians. Vaccination of animals is a critical step in preventing infection and protecting public health."1 References CDC: rabies exposures have increased, including from variety of species. AVMA. September 11, 2026. analysis.time: September 14, 2026 (publication date); the CDC advisory was issued on September 10, 2026, and the incidents were reported from July through August 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Multiple US states, including North Carolina, Maryland, New Jersey, and New Hampshire; the affected population includes humans and animals, with specific incidents involving goats, beavers, raccoons, and foxes or fishers.
analysis.event: Several rabies exposure incidents were reported across multiple states, including an outbreak linked to a traveling petting zoo in North Carolina and attacks by rabid animals in Maryland, New Jersey, and New Hampshire. The AVMA reiterated its rabies vaccination policy following a CDC advisory on increased human exposures and PEP administration errors.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: At least 8 state health departments reported increased rabies PEP use, administration errors, or both over the past 3 months. In North Carolina, more than 260 people were advised to receive PEP. As of September 2, 2026, rabies vaccine and human rabies immune globulin use had increased by 33% and 76%, respectively, compared to the same period in 2025. Annually, about 1.4 million people seek medical care after suspected contact with rabid animals, and approximately 100,000 receive PEP. Fewer than 10 human rabies deaths are reported annually in the US.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC issued a health advisory on September 10, 2026, and health departments reported increased PEP use and errors. The AVMA reiterated its vaccination policy and endorsed the 2016 Compendium of Animal Rabies Prevention and Control. The situation is under investigation, with no confirmed cases of rabies in humans or animals reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.brief_en: The AVMA reported several rabies exposure incidents across multiple US states, including an outbreak linked to a traveling petting zoo in North Carolina where over 260 people were advised to receive post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). Other incidents involved rabid beavers in Maryland, a raccoon bite in New Jersey, and an attack by a suspected gray fox or fisher in New Hampshire. The CDC issued a health advisory on September 10, 2026, highlighting a nationwide increase in human rabies exposures and errors in PEP administration. From July through August 2026, the CDC received 17% more rabies-related inquiries than in the same period in 2025. news.title_zh: 在新的 CDC 咨询中,AVMA 详细介绍了最近的 狂犬病 暴露事件,重申了 疫苗接种 政策
news.source_body_en: The AVMA reported several rabies exposure incidents across multiple US states, including an outbreak linked to a traveling petting zoo in North Carolina where over 260 people were advised to receive post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). Other incidents involved rabid beavers in Maryland, a raccoon bite in New Jersey, and an attack by a suspected gray fox or fisher in New Hampshire. The CDC issued a health advisory on September 10, 2026, highlighting a nationwide increase in human rabies exposures and errors in PEP administration. The AVMA reiterated its vaccination policy and endorsed the 2016 Compendium of Animal Rabies Prevention and Control. While no confirmed human rabies cases were reported, the incidents underscore the importance of vaccination and PEP in preventing the spread of rabies. news.content_zh: AVMA 报告了美国多个州发生的多起 狂犬病 暴露事件,其中包括与北卡罗来纳州一家流动宠物动物园有关的 狂犬病 事件,该动物园建议超过 260 人接受 暴露后预防 (PEP)。其他事件还包括马里兰州的海狸狂犬病、新泽西州的浣熊咬伤事件以及新罕布什尔州疑似灰狐或渔民的袭击事件。CDC 于 2026 年 9 月 10 日发布健康咨询,强调全国范围内人类 狂犬病 暴露的增加以及 PEP 管理中的错误。从2026年7月到2026年8月,CDC收到的与狂犬病相关的询问比2025年同期增加了17%。截至2026年9月2日,狂犬病、疫苗和免疫球蛋白产品的使用量分别增加了33%和76%。AVMA 重申了其 疫苗接种 政策,并批准了 2016 年动物 狂犬病 预防和控制纲要。虽然没有报告确诊的人类 狂犬病 病例,但这些事件强调了 疫苗接种 和 PEP 在防止 狂犬病 传播方面的重要性。目前情况仍在调查中,卫生部门正在监测 PEP 使用的增加和管理错误。
