news.content_title: CDC Warns of Rising Rabies Cases: Essential Tips from a Veterinarian to Protect Your Pet
news.content: On September 10, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a Health Alert Network (HAN) Health Advisory announcing a concerning increase in rabies cases reported nationwide. We spoke with Dr. Lindsay Kendrick, Hospital Director at VEG ER for Pets, to learn how pet parents can keep their furry friends safe amidst the worrisome news. She shares her best advice for protecting dogs, outdoor cats , and indoor pets from rabies exposure, and explains exactly why rabies is nearly 100% fatal once symptoms begin. In July and August, the CDC received 17% more rabies reports than in the same period last year. Several spots around the nation are experiencing a dramatic increase in local cases, though pet parents country-wide are encouraged to stay vigilant and proactive. Related: Dogs Face a Backyard Danger This Week That Pet Parents Can Test For In Seconds Rhode Island, New York, South Carolina, and California are just a few of the affected areas, which is why it's important for pet parents to stay informed of the local news. However, Dr. Kendrick reminds families that rabies can affect any mammal , so prevention and prompt action are essential. Pet parents know that rabies is a terrifying illness, but how exactly does it work? "The virus travels through the nerves to the brain," Dr. Kendrick explains. "By the time symptoms appear, it has already caused severe damage to the nervous system, and there is no reliable treatment that can stop it at that point. Prevention and quick action after a possible exposure are so important. There is a window of time to intervene before symptoms begin, but once they do, the disease is nearly always fatal." A veterinarian examining a cat.Guillermo Spelucin Runciman / Getty Images Because the rabies virus is carried in saliva, most family pets who become infected with rabies get it through a bite from another animal. However, Dr. Kendrick reminds, "A scratch can be a risk if it's contaminated with saliva, and virus transmission can occur if saliva from an infected animal gets into an open wound or into the eyes, nose, or mouth. Simply touching an animal or coming into contact with blood, urine, or feces is not generally considered a rabies exposure." "If a person was bitten, scratched, or had saliva get into an open wound, eye, nose, or mouth," she continues, "they should wash the area thoroughly with soap and water and seek human medical advice immediately." Although rabies "doesn't always look like the 'foaming at the mouth' picture people imagine," pet parents can learn to recognize the early symptoms of rabies. Ideally, pets would receive help immediately after a bite, before symptoms begin, but this could also help people identify whether a wild animal is potentially rabid. Early symptoms of rabies in cats and dogs include: As the disease progresses, symptoms can include: sensitivity to light, sound, or touch If you see these symptoms in a pet following a wildlife encounter, do not touch their mouth or saliva. This means staying vigilant when your pet is around wild animals, whether they're taking a potty break in the backyard or going for a walk. If a potentially rabid animal enters your home, though, do your best to separate your pet from it and contact Animal Control for guidance on next steps. 🐶 SIGN UP to get "pawsitivity" delivered right to your inbox with inspiring & entertaining stories about our furry & feathered friends 🐾🐾 In case of outdoor encounters, Dr. Kendrick says, "Don't try to grab the wild animal or separate the animals with your bare hands. Get your pet safely away from the animal, avoid contact with saliva, and call your vet right away. The pet should be examined even if you don't see an obvious wound and even if they are vaccinated. Small punctures, especially bat bites, can be easy to miss." As for being proactive about rabies protection, these are Dr. Kendrick's best tips: Keep pets' rabies vaccinations up to date Avoid leaving trash outside that may attract wildlife Don't let pets approach wild animals Do not handle wild animals yourself With a little knowledge and attentiveness (and Dr. Kendrick's helpful tips), anyone can keep their beloved pets safe from this horrible illness. Instead of being worried, be aware! This story was originally published by PetHelpful on Sep 17, 2026, where it first appeared in the Pet News section. news.content_zh: CDC 于 2026 年 9 月 10 日发布了健康警报网络 (HAN) 健康咨询,强调了全国范围内 狂犬病 病例的令人担忧的增加。7 月和 8 月,狂犬病 报告数量与 2025 年同期相比增加了 17%。这一增长在罗德岛州、纽约州、南卡罗来纳州和加利福尼亚州等几个州都出现了。VEG ER for Pets 医院院长 Lindsay Kendrick 强调了 狂犬病 预防和在潜在接触后迅速采取行动的重要性。她解释说,一旦出现症状,狂犬病 几乎 100% 致命,因为病毒会通过神经传播到大脑,对神经系统造成严重损害。敦促宠物父母及时更新宠物的 疫苗接种,避免接触野生动物,如果有任何潜在的接触,请立即寻求兽医建议。疾病预防控制中心正在监测情况,并建议公众保持警惕并积极主动地保护他们的宠物免受 狂犬病 的侵害。

By Michaela Harris Published: Sep. 16, 2026 at 12:05 AM UTC Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google HEALTH MINUTE (CBS) - Federal health officials issued warnings about an increase in rabies cases. Rabies is a viral disease that is nearly 100% fatal, but preventable when treatment is started right away before symptoms start. Confirmed cases of rabies in animals have many communities concerned. The CDC is issuing an official health advisory after recent increases in human exposures to rabid animals. From July through August, the agency received 17% more inquiries related to rabies than the same time last year, including reports of mass exposure events like petting zoos. Zak Mertz is the chief executive officer of the New England Wildlife Center and on a task force combatting rabies in Massachusetts. He said rising cases are likely due to a population increase in the animals that frequently carry the disease. The task force is using helicopters to drop edible vaccine packets in an effort to vaccinate animals in the wild. “It’s no reason to panic but it’s a good reminder that rabies is out there,” said Mertz. It’s estimated more than a million people in the U.S. seek medical care after contact with an animal. About 100,000 receive preventive treatment for potential exposure. The CDC is also warning about reports from several health departments about errors related to treatment after exposure. The CDC recommends the public keep their distance from wildlife, keep pets up to date on rabies vaccines and away from wildlife, wash a wound right away if bitten or scratched by wildlife, and talk with a doctor or public health professional about their risk and whether they might need rabies-related care. Experts advise to never approach an animal that appears sick, injured or dead, especially animals that are usually active at night, like bats and raccoons, if seen during the day. news.content_title: Rabies vaccine baits to be distributed via helicopter across Western Pennsylvania
news.content: Rabies vaccine baits to be distributed via helicopter across Western Pennsylvania The U.S. Department of Agriculture is distributing oral rabies vaccine baits across western Pennsylvania this week as part of an ongoing effort to combat wildlife rabies. More than 225,000 baits are being distributed via helicopter across Allegheny County and in portions of Beaver, Lawrence and Washington counties. The program aims to stop the westward spread of the rabies virus, which is most frequently carried and transmitted by raccoons. The baiting program is part of the USDA National Rabies Management Program, which has distributed oral rabies vaccine baits in parts of Pennsylvania using aerial drops and vehicles since 2001. The baits emit a scent that attracts targeted wildlife such as raccoons, which eat the bait and become vaccinated against rabies. Rabies infects the central nervous system in mammals and is almost always fatal if exposure is left untreated. Annual costs associated with rabies detection, prevention and control in the United States exceed $600 million. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about 90% of reported rabies cases in the U.S. occur in wild animals. Health officials state that humans and domestic animals cannot contract rabies from touching the baits, but residents are asked to leave them undisturbed. Pets that consume a bait may experience a temporary upset stomach due to the richness of the attractant. Anyone who touches a bait should immediately rinse the area with warm water and soap. Public health officials also urge residents to avoid feeding or contacting wildlife and to keep pet rabies vaccinations up to date. Helicopter distribution of the baits is expected to last approximately one week, weather permitting. Download the FREE WPXI News app for breaking news alerts. news.content: Search Fox Weather The FOX Weather App Learn More Watch Live Weather News How to Watch Extreme Weather Learn Local Weather Space Lifestyle Video America's Weather Team Podcast Deals Lifestyle Published September 14, 2026 5:47pm EDT CDC warns of rising rabies exposures across the US as deadly disease threat grows The CDC said it received 17% more rabies-related inquiries from July through August 2026 than during the same time period in 2025. By Alexandra Myers Source FOX Weather Facebook Twitter Email Copy Link FILE: What is rabies? Rabies FAQs. Did you know that you can get rabies even if you were not bitten? THE TAKEAWAY The CDC warns that human rabies exposures are on the rise across the U.S. The CDC said it received 17% more rabies-related inquiries from July through August 2026 than during the same time period in 2025. At least eight state health departments reported an increase in administering post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for rabies. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is warning that human rabies exposures are on the rise across the U.S. Since July, multiple cities have reported local increases in human rabies exposures involving known rabies vectors and animals that less commonly carry the disease. THIS 1,600-POUND OCEAN GIANT JUST WENT SOMEWHERE NO OTHER OCEARCH-TAGGED SHARK HAS EVER BEEN The CDC said it received 17% more rabies-related inquiries from July through August 2026 than during the same time period in 2025. Signage outside the Center for Disease Control (CDC) headquarters in Atlanta, Georgia, US. (Megan Varner/Bloomberg / Getty Images) During the same time frame, at least eight state health departments reported an increase in administering post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for rabies, PEP administration errors or both. SOMETHING IS LURKING BENEATH THE EVERGLADES — AND FLORIDA’S FROGS AND SALAMANDERS ARE AT RISK Typically, about 1.4 million people in the U.S. seek medical care each year after animal contact, and approximately 100,000 people receive rabies PEP. However, according to weekly pharmacy data as of Sept. 2, 2026, the use of the two rabies vaccines and two immunoglobulins licensed in the U.S. increased by an estimated 33% and 76%, respectively, compared to the same time last year. Health officials in North Carolina are warning residents who had contact with baby goats at a mobile petting zoo after three of the animals tested positive for rabies. (Lokman Ilhan/Anadolu Agency / Getty Images) Just this summer, more than 300 people in North Carolina were exposed to rabid baby goats at a mobile petting zoo. At least 213 residents were recommended post-exposure prophylaxis to help prevent infection. BABY GOATS TEST POSITIVE FOR RABIES AS OFFICIALS SEEK PEOPLE WHO MAY HAVE BEEN EXPOSED Rabies is a zoonotic viral disease that is nearly 100% fatal once symptoms begin. However, the disease can be prevented when PEP is administered before symptoms start. Typically, about 1.4 million people in the U.S. seek medical care each year after animal contact, and approximately 100,000 people receive rabies PEP. (Abby Drey/Centre Daily Times/Tribune News Service / Getty Images) Rabies spreads to humans and other animals through bites, scratches or contact with infected oral secretions. The disease ultimately affects the central nervous system, leading to encephalitis and death if medical care is not received promptly after exposure and before symptoms begin. HERE'S EVERYTHING YOU NEED TO KNOW ABOUT FLESH-EATING PARASITE IN THE US AS CASES TRIPLE IN SIZE Although there isn't a shortage of human rabies vaccines or human rabies immunoglobulin in the U.S., the CDC is reminding medical professionals to administer PEP appropriately. A "Department of Health and Human Services" sign outside the Center for Disease Control (CDC) headquarters in Atlanta, Georgia. (Megan Varner/Bloomberg / Getty Images) Errors in rabies risk assessment and PEP administration could result in unnecessary treatment, potential adverse effects and avoidable costs. HOW TO WATCH FOX WEATHER A typical course of PEP can cost between $11,000 and $14,000 per person. For more information, visit cdc.gov. Tags US Health Animals Wildlife Safety Stay22 Lifestyle

Closed Captioning Information Manage Emails Apps Careers Search Q2News/ ktvq UCN2IWwjVxh4vOnMbnjiM8Hw 19 WX Alerts News Montana Politics Montana Ag Network America 250 Your Health Matters Indian Country Positively Montana My MTN Contests More + Quick Links + News Montana Politics Montana Ag Network America 250 Your Health Matters Indian Country Positively Montana My MTN Contests News Actions Facebook Tweet Email Yellowstone County sees uptick in human interaction with bats Prev Next Courtesy Photo Riley Buttram's foot after being bit by a bat By: Hannah Pedeferri Posted BILLINGS, Mont. — Montana health officials are seeing a spike in rabies cases. Thirteen bats have tested positive for rabies in Montana this year. Riverstone Health says bat encounters are up this year. The county has tracked 11 incidents so far — eight of them involving human contact. That is already double the human interactions reported last year. Watch the full story below: Yellowstone County sees uptick in human interaction with bats Stacie Pannell, communicable disease program manager at RiverStone Health, said an "interaction" does not always mean a bite. It can include a scratch — or even waking up in a room with a bat. "Were they bitten? Were they scratched? We don't know," Pannell said Friday. "After somebody has an interaction with a bat, we recommend post-exposure prophylaxis for rabies. That treatment is extensive. Pannell described what it involves. "They get immune globulin to start with. It's called HRAIG, or Human Rabies Immune Globulin, and the rabies vaccination. And then they get that rabies vaccination again on day three, seven, and fourteen," Pannell said. Pannell believes more people are reporting these encounters because awareness around rabies is growing. "I do think that it's made people more aware that bats do pose, or can pose, a danger for their health," Pannell said. Riley Buttram knows firsthand how painful that treatment can be. A bat bit her during a camping trip in 2018, and she describes the experience vividly. "It just felt like they were sticking a toothpick up my foot," Buttram said. "It was horrible." The bite happened in seconds. She reached into a car to grab a jacket. "I couldn't get it from one side of the car, so I went to the other side and grabbed it, and then I looked down and there was a bat, and it like bit me on my foot," Buttram said. She barely felt the bite, but she knew she could not ignore it. "We went to the hospital, and for precaution, they gave me seven shots in my foot because that's where it bit me," Buttram said. That was just the start. "Two of my thighs and two of my arms, and then they sent the bat off to get tested, and it did have rabies," Buttram said. The treatment was so intense that medical staff had to physically restrain her. "They had to hold me down because the needles are so long," Buttram said. Eight years later, Buttram still remembers it clearly — and she feels for those in Yellowstone County now going through the same thing. Her message is simple: don't take the risk. "If we wouldn't have kept the bat, we would have been like, 'Oh, okay, maybe she didn't get bit.' I would have gotten rabies. I could have died," Buttram said. supplementary_news.content: Minnesota News Rabies detected in southern Minnesota cow Nine people recommended for post rabies exposure treatment By Clay Schuldt September 19, 2026 4 min read Trending The Minnesota Board of Animal Health confirmed a cow in southern Minnesota has tested positive for rabies. The Board of Animal Health stated rabies was found in a Hereford heifer located in Brown County, though the exact location of the animal or its owners is not being released. Board of Animal Health Communication Director Michael Crusan said unless there is a threat to the wider population and wildlife, the board will only identify the county where the infection was identified. In this case, there is no risk of infection moving off the premise. Board of Animal Health did confirm the owner of the cow first noticed symptoms in the cow on Sept. 1. The owner observed the heifer laying flat on the grown with its head down. A veterinarian observed the animal the same day and the owner had administered oral medication with bare hands. Another veterinarian examined the animal the following day and also gave it oral medication without wearing gloves. A third veterinarian examined the animal on Sept. 3 and noticed it had uncoordinated hind legs, was high-stepping, vocalizing, hyper-salivating and had a high temperature. Since these symptoms match those of rabies, the animal was euthanized to perform a rabies test. In order to test an animal for rabies, the animal’s brain must be examined. This test was conducted at the Minnesota Department of Health Public Health Laboratory. Brain tissue tested positive for the rabies virus on Sept. 8. Public health officials have recommended that nine people who came in contact with the animal and is saliva seek rabies post-exposure prophylaxis as a preventative measure. The board quarantined 13 other cows on the same farm so they can be monitored for rabies symptoms. More than 40 cattle on the property will also be watched for any signs of rabies symptoms. A horse on the property was also possibly exposed, but is up-to-date on its rabies vaccinations, along with three vaccinated dogs. Two unvaccinated barn cats that were likely exposed to rabies were euthanized. Once a domestic animal is exposed, it can take anywhere from two to 26 weeks for symptoms of rabies to develop, depending on the location of the bite and the amount of the virus that enters the body. Most domestic animals that show symptoms will die within three to 12 weeks. Dr. Katie Cornille, senior veterinarian at the state Board of Animal Health, said symptoms of rabies infection could include any strange behavior that hinted at neurological damage. This could present as poor coordination, unusual vocalizations, difficulty in swallowing and hypersalivation. The heifer that tested positive did exhibit most of this symptoms. Cornille said rabies eventually travels to the brain, causing encephalopathy and eventually leading to death. Unfortunately, by the time an animal begins to show symptoms, it is already too late. Cornille said there is a post-rabies exposure treatment for humans, but for animals, the procedure is to vaccinate. The rabies virus is typically spread by bite or saliva. In Minnesota, the most common animals to spread rabies are skunks and bats. In this specific case, it is believed that a skunk was responsible for transmitting the virus to the cow. Crusan said in this incident skunks were seen on the property and adjacent property around the time the infection was reported. Cornille said most animals can contract rabies. In other parts of the country, foxes or raccoons might be the main spread of rabies. But in Minnesota, bats and skunks tend to be the main vector species. "It is not common in cows," Cornille said. "That's why it is concerning, but it’s not unheard of for a cow to be infected." Crusan said that according to the Board of Animal Health database, this recent incident is the first rabies detection in the state for 2026. The last time a cow tested positive for rabies in Minnesota was in 2024. Cornille said rabies is something the public should be aware of, but warned against intense alarm. She recommended the public follow best practices. It is recommended that domesticated animals be vaccinated against the virus, which is mandated in many communities. She also recommended securing homes and barns from wildlife and keeping a safe distance from wildlife that are acting abnormal. Anyone with concerns about a specific animal is encouraged to contact animal control

supplementary_news.content: A Brown County Hereford heifer tested positive for the rabies virus, the Minnesota Board of Animal Health said Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. Brooke Bobendrier /Real Ag Stock By Noah Fish September 17, 2026 at 3:03 PM Nine people, including two minor children and five veterinary workers, were advised to seek rabies post-exposure treatment after a Brown County Hereford heifer tested positive for the virus, the Minnesota Board of Animal Health said Thursday. The animal tested positive Sept. 8 at the Minnesota Department of Health Public Health Laboratory, according to a press release dated Sept. 17 . The health department recommended treatment for the owner, the owner's daughter, two minor children, two of the veterinarians who examined the animal and three veterinary technicians who assisted. All may have been exposed to the animal's saliva. Keep Watching S12E38-WEB-PKG5 According to the board, rabies is a preventable viral disease of mammals that attacks the central nervous system, causing encephalopathy and death. It is most often transmitted through the bite of a rabid animal, though saliva entering the eyes, nose, mouth or a fresh open wound can also expose a person. Post-exposure treatment consists of human rabies immune globulin and a series of rabies vaccinations given at specified intervals. According to the release, the owner noticed the heifer behaving oddly Sept. 1, lying flat with its head down, and after a veterinarian examined it that day, the owner administered oral medication with bare hands. A second veterinarian examined the animal the next day and also gave oral medication without gloves. On Sept. 3, a third veterinarian found the animal had uncoordinated hind legs, was high-stepping, vocalizing, hypersalivating and had a high temperature. It was euthanized and its head was removed for testing. "When we see livestock acting strangely, rabies may not be the first thing people think of to explain the behavior," said Steve Kivisto, the senior veterinarian who leads the board's rabies program, in the release. "Given the severity of the disease, it's better to assume an animal is infected until proven otherwise, and to be sure to take the proper precautions and use the correct personal protective equipment when working with a rabies suspect animal." Read more livestock news Record diesel, interest rate hike and soybean sales hold markets Friday 1d ago Watch live from the Agweek 360 Building at Big Iron: Hive Mind 2d ago Watch live from the Agweek 360 Building at Big Iron: Will the U.S. Cattle Herd Expand? 2d ago The board, which holds unvaccinated exposed animals 45 to 180 days, said that it has quarantined 13 cows, while more than 40 cattle will be kept under observation. A horse on the property was possibly exposed but is current on its vaccinations and will be watched, along with three vaccinated dogs. Two unvaccinated barn cats with likely exposure were euthanized. Skunks and bats are the natural carriers of rabies in Minnesota, according to the release, and wild animals, especially bats, account for most of the state's reported cases each year. Fewer than 15% of cases reported annually occur in domestic species, most commonly cattle, cats and dogs. "Numerous skunks were observed earlier this year on a neighboring plot of land owned by a relative that adjoins the area where the heifer was held," read the press release, but it was not stated whether any of the skunks were tested and did not identify a confirmed source of the heifer's infection. Rabies in Minnesota cattle has climbed since 2024, when seven animals tested positive statewide, up from the three that tested positive in 2023. In June, the Minnesota Board of Animal Health joined animal health officials in Iowa, South Dakota and Nebraska in a notification that counted 10 rabid cattle across three states since 2024, with seven of them being dairy animals. The four-state region logged 25 rabid skunks over the same period. Livestock are generally tested only after someone reports an animal sick, and the board said the real count is probably higher than what gets confirmed. Clinical signs vary by species and by the strain of the virus, but most infected animals show behavioral changes or neurological signs. According to the board, cattle may bellow frequently and have trouble walking and swallowing. Incubation in domestic animals runs two to 26 weeks depending on where the animal was bitten and how much virus entered the body, and most show signs and die within three to 12 weeks. Clusters of rabies have happened in recent years in the state, as five of 35 steers on a Stearns County dairy farm developed neurologic signs over four weeks in May 2024, according to a report published in December by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Three were confirmed positive for the North Central skunk variant. Investigators concluded that a single rabid skunk had likely bitten several steers penned together, though they could not rule out transmission between the steers. The herd's 45-day quarantine was extended to 120 days as more animals fell ill. Twelve unvaccinated farm cats were euthanized. Five people were referred for treatment in that case. Direct medical and veterinary costs ran about $35,000, roughly $32,000 of it treatment for four family members. Farm business insurance and the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Livestock Indemnity Program generally do not cover those losses. Vaccinating cattle costs $12 to $30 a head, the board said in June. "Vaccination is very effective and directly saves the lives of exposed animals," Kivisto said. "Vaccines are readily available for dogs, cats, ferrets, cattle, horses and sheep." Vaccines are responsible for a substantial decrease in human rabies cases over the past century, the board said. The board recommends producers vaccinate animals in their care, keep strays and wildlife away from pets and livestock, avoid approaching unfamiliar or wild animals, and report strays or animals acting unusually to local animal control. Producers can reach the board at 651-201-6808. The health department's line for human exposure questions is 651-201-5414. The CDC is warning of a summer spike in rabies exposures, and the state of Illinois is experiencing similar issues The Illinois Department of Public Health (IDPH) says it's seen a "higher-than-normal rabies call volume and bat submission for this time of year," but the agency says the numbers are not alarming. As of September 9, the Rabies surveillance map shows 61 animals have tested positive so far in 2026, an increase over the past two years. Stream NBC 5 for free, 24/7, wherever you are. WATCH HERE It comes as the CDC reported a spike in rabies cases at the federal level among animals this summer, which has led to a rise in human exposures across the country. In a new health advisory, the CDC urged doctors to be on the lookout for possible exposures and to administer vaccines and treatments as needed. Rabies is a viral disease that is deadly if people don't receive medical care before symptoms start, according to the CDC. Rabies spreads primarily through bites or scratches from an infected animal, and the animals most frequently found with rabies in the U.S. are bats, skunks, raccoons, and foxes. From July through August, the CDC said it received 17% more rabies-related inquiries than during the same period last year and also received reports from at least eight state health departments about the increased use of rabies shots, or of errors in the administration of the post-exposure regimen. Local Austin 42 minutes ago Chicago police investigating after girl, 14, critically injured in Austin shooting Bronzeville 2 hours ago Suspects sought after 41 cars broken into in Bronzeville parking lot According to IDPH, the CDC has not notified the agency which states are included. The disease is rare in people in the United States, with fewer than 10 deaths reported each year. Pet vaccinations, which are required by law in all 50 states, have significantly reduced the risk. "Even if your pets are indoor or monitored closely, going on walks or being in the backyard, they could be at risk for coming into contact with a rabid bat for example," said Dr. Emily Winson, an associate veterinarian at West Loop Veterinary Care. "Our indoor cats that never go outside, unfortunately rabid bats do try to seek shelter indoors. If indoor cats are not up to date with vaccines, they could be at risk if a bat gets inside through a small hole or crevice in your home." Anyone in a room with a bat is encouraged to contact their healthcare provider and animal control to remove the bat and test it. "Never touch a wild animal, whether it looks healthy or injured, it's best to leave it to the professionals and call animal control," said Winson. Free rabies vaccines are available for cats and dogs through the Cook County Department of Animal and Rabies Control at various locations. Health officials say multiple people have received treatment after a rabid skunk was confirmed in the Kootenay Lake area. The rabies virus is found in the saliva and nervous system tissue of an infected animal. Rabies is usually spread through a bite or, less commonly, a scratch from an infected animal. Rabies virus is not transmitted through exposure to the spray, urine or feces of infected skunks in B.C. Bats are the only known reservoirs of rabies, meaning they can carry the disease and pass it on without showing signs of the disease themselves. Occasional spillovers to other animal species have occurred in B.C. Rabies infections in people are extremely rare in B.C. and Canada. Infections are usually fatal, but preventable when vaccines are administered promptly after an exposure. supplementary_news.content: Local Sports High School Huddle Scene Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTH CDC raises rabies concerns in US. Comes after NC baby goats test positive Iris Seaton Asheville Citizen Times Sept. 15, 2026, 5:02 a.m. ET The CDC has warned of a recent rise in reports of human exposures to potentially rabid animals. Rabies is nearly 100% fatal once symptoms begin, but it is preventable with post-exposure medication. While any mammal can carry rabies, it is most commonly found in wild animals like bats, raccoons, and foxes. A notice issued by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has warned of a rise in reports of human exposures to rabid or possibly rabid animals in recent months. The Health Alert Network Health Advisory was issued Sept. 10. The alert came weeks after the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services issued a news release regarding a potential rabies exposure among four baby goats at Farm Adventures in Harmony on Aug. 27, as reported by the Citizen Times. The infected baby goats were taken to at least seven North Carolina counties as part of a traveling petting zoo, resulting in potentially hundreds of exposures across the state. The incident was one of several mass exposure events reported in recent months by the CDC. Are rabies cases rising in the U.S.? While a rise in confirmed cases of rabies in humans has not been confirmed, a Health Alert Network Health Advisory was issued by the CDC on Sept. 10 in response to increased reports of human exposures to rabid or possibly rabid animals and errors in the administration of rabies post-exposure prophylaxis, also known as "PEP." According to the CDC, multiple U.S. jurisdictions have reported local increases in human rabies exposures since July 2026, particularly in exposures involving known rabies vectors or animals in which rabies is less commonly reported. The alert noted that health departments "can help clinicians who provide rabies vaccination in their jurisdictions stay aware of the importance of rabies risk assessments before administering PEP," working to ensure that PEP is only given when appropriate and that human rabies immune globulin or "HRIG" and rabies vaccines are administered according to the proper recommendations. What medications are given to treat rabies in humans? As explained in the CDC alert, rabies is almost 100% fatal, but is preventable when preventative medications are given appropriately before symptoms begin. Rabies PEP recommendations from the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices include: Wound care A dose of HRIG, with U.S. approved medications including KEDRAB and HyperRab A rabies vaccine - U.S. approved vaccines include Imovax (HDCV) and RabAvert (PCECV) - given at the time of the first medical visit, with follow-up doses given on days 3, 7 and 14 after the first dose The CDC reported that according to weekly pharmacy data from Sept. 2, utilization for U.S. licensed rabies vaccines and rabies immunoglobulins increased by an estimated 33% and 76%, respectively, compared with the same time period last year. Can rabies be cured? The Cleveland Clinic explains that there are no approved treatments for rabies once symptoms have begun. Worms & Germs, a blog devoted to safe pet ownership, reported Jan. 12 that only 34 documented cases of rabies survival have been reported, with an even smaller number of people having survived without long-term neurological deficits. In particular, a treatment regimen called the "Milwaukee protocol," in which anesthetic drugs used to put the patient in a coma and slow brain function are combined with antivirals and intensive care, has been successfully used to treat rabies. Rabies cases in the U.S. Between July and August 2026, the CDC received 17% more rabies-related inquiries during the same period in 2025, including reports of mass exposure events such as the event reported in the Tar Heel State in late August 2026. The CDC reported that each year, an estimated 1.4 million people in the U.S. seek medical care after animal contact and undergo evaluation, and roughly 100,000 people receive rabies PEP following a potential exposure. Rabies cases in North Carolina A recent N.C. Department of Health and Human Services statement noted that human rabies infections are "extremely rare" in the U.S., and no human cases have been reported in the state since 2011. How is rabies spread? The N.C. DHHS states that rabies can be spread from wild animals to pets and people primarily through bites, scratches, or infected saliva touching broken skin or mucous membranes. What animals can carry rabies? Though any mammal can carry and spread rabies, Mayo Clinic states that pets and farm most likely to transmit the rabies virus include cats, cows, dogs, ferrets, goats and horses. Wild animals most likely to spread the virus include bats, beavers, coyotes, foxes, monkeys, raccoons, skunks and woodchucks. Iris Seaton is the trending news reporter for the Asheville Citizen Times, part of the USA TODAY Network. Reach her at iseaton@citizentimes.com. CDC Highlights Significant Increase in U.S. Rabies Exposures and Anti-Rabies Immunoglobulin Utilization; Kamada Confirms Sufficient KedRAB® Supply to Meet Increased Demand Kamada Ltd. Thu, September 17, 2026 at 6:00 AM CDT 7 min read KMDA +2.08% KMDA +2.08% Kamada Ltd. U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Reports a Significant Year-Over-Year Increase in Nationwide Rabies Exposures and Rabies Immunoglobulin Utilization KedRAB is One of Only Two FDA-Approved Anti-Rabies Immunoglobulin Products in the U.S. Market Estimated at $200 Million Annually Kamada's Manufacturing Capacity and Supply Availability Positioned to Support Increased Demand REHOVOT, Israel, and HOBOKEN, N.J., Sept. 17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Kamada Ltd. (NASDAQ: KMDA; TASE: KMDA.TA) (the "Company"), a global biopharmaceutical company with a portfolio of marketed products indicated for rare and serious conditions and a leader in the specialty plasma-derived therapies field, today confirmed that it maintains sufficient KedRAB® supply and manufacturing capacity to meet increased demand for the product in the United States. The confirmation follows a Health Advisory published by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on September 10, 2026, reporting a significant nationwide year-over-year increase in human rabies exposures and the use of rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). The CDC Health Advisory is available at: https://www.cdc.gov/han/php/notices/han00533.html. In light of this increase in end-user utilization described in the CDC advisory, Kamada confirms it has the inventory and manufacturing capacity to support the continued supply of KedRAB, a human rabies immune globulin developed and manufactured by Kamada, which is one of only two FDA-approved anti-rabies immunoglobulin products indicated for PEP treatment in the U.S. The product is supplied to the U.S. market via the Company's U.S. commercialization partner, Kedrion Biopharma Inc. "Kamada is a global leader in human rabies prevention using immunoglobulin and we remain committed to delivering reliable, uninterrupted supply of KedRAB to meet the needs of patients and clinicians across the United States," said Amir London, Chief Executive Officer of Kamada. "Our long-standing successful partnership with Kedrion, together with our vertically integrated supply chain, and the recent FDA approval of our in-house rabies testing lab, position us to respond to this year-over-year increase in demand while maintaining the consistency and quality that this lifesaving therapeutic requires." Rabies is a deadly viral disease that attacks the brain and nervous system of mammals, including humans. The CDC estimates that approximately 1.4 million people in the United States seek medical care for a possible rabies exposure each year, of whom approximately 100,000 receive PEP treatment. Kamada estimates the total U.S. market for rabies immunoglobulin products at approximately $200 million annually. Story Continues INDICATION AND SELECTED IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION INDICATION: KEDRAB is a human rabies immune globulin (HRIG) indicated for passive, transient post-exposure prophylaxis of rabies infection to persons of all ages when given immediately after contact with a rabid or possibly rabid animal. KEDRAB should be administered concurrently with a full course of rabies vaccine. IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION ABOUT KedRAB: Severe hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, may occur with KedRAB. IgA deficient patients with antibodies against IgA are at greater risk. Have epinephrine available immediately to treat any acute severe hypersensitivity reactions. KedRAB administration may interfere with the development of an immune response to live attenuated virus vaccines. If feasible, delay immunization with the measles vaccine for 4 months, and other live attenuated virus vaccines for three months, after KedRAB administration. A transient rise of the various passively transferred antibodies in the patient's blood may result in misleading positive results of serologic tests after KedRAB administration. Passive transmission of antibodies to erythrocyte antigens, e.g., A, B, and D, may interfere with serologic tests for red cell antibodies such as the antiglobulin test (Coombs' test). KedRAB is made from human plasma donors and may carry a risk of transmitting infectious agents, e.g., viruses, the variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (vCJD) agent and, theoretically, the Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) agent. To report SUSPECTED ADVERSE REACTIONS, contact Kedrion Biopharma Inc. at 1-855-353-7466 or the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088 or www.fda.gov/medwatch. I.D. Code: KAM.001-26 About Kamada Kamada Ltd. (the "Company") is a global biopharmaceutical company with a portfolio of marketed products indicated for rare and serious conditions and a leader in the specialty plasma-derived therapies field. FIMI Opportunity Funds, the leading private equity firm in Israel, is the Company's controlling shareholder, beneficially owning approximately 38% of the outstanding ordinary shares. The Company's strategy is focused on driving profitable growth through four primary growth pillars: First, organic growth of its commercial portfolio, including continued investment in the commercialization and life cycle management of its proprietary products, consisting of six FDA-approved specialty plasma-derived products: KEDRAB®, GLASSIA®, CYTOGAM®, VARIZIG®, WINRHO SDF® and HEPAGAM B®, as well as KAMRAB®, and two equine-based anti-snake venom products. Second, distribution of third-parties' pharmaceutical products in Israel & the MENA region through in-licensing partnerships, including the launch of several biosimilar products in Israel. Third, the Company is ramping up its plasma collection operations to support revenue growth through the sale of normal source plasma to other plasma-derived manufacturers, and to support its increasing demand for hyper-immune plasma. The Company currently owns three FDA-approved operating plasma collection centers in the United States, in Beaumont, Houston, and San Antonio, Texas. Fourth, the Company aims to secure new mergers and acquisitions, business development, in-licensing and/or collaboration opportunities, which are anticipated to enhance the Company's marketed products portfolio and leverage its financial strength and existing commercial infrastructure to drive long-term profitable growth. The Company is leveraging its manufacturing, research and development expertise to advance the development and commercialization of additional product candidates, targeting areas of significant unmet medical need. Cautionary Note Regarding Forward-Looking Statements This release includes forward-looking statements within the meaning of Section 21E of the U.S. Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended, and the safe harbor provisions of the U.S. Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Forward-looking statements are statements that are not historical facts, including statements regarding: (1) the sufficiency of the Company's KedRAB inventory and manufacturing capacity to meet current and future U.S. demand; and (2) expectations regarding continued or increased demand for KedRAB in the United States. Forward-looking statements are based on Kamada's current knowledge and its present beliefs and expectations regarding possible future events and are subject to risks, uncertainties and assumptions. Actual results and the timing of events could differ materially from those anticipated in these forward-looking statements as a result of several factors, including, but not limited to: the unpredictable and seasonal nature of rabies exposure trends and the possibility that reported increases in demand do not continue or recur; Kamada's reliance on Kedrion as its sole distributor of KedRAB in the United States and any change in that relationship; Kamada's ability to manufacture sufficient quantities of KedRAB and to obtain adequate quantities of hyper-immune plasma and other raw materials on a timely basis; competition from other rabies immunoglobulin and rabies biologic products; the evolving nature of the conflicts in the Middle East and the impact of such conflicts in Israel, the Middle East and the rest of the world; the impact of these conflicts on market conditions and the general economic, industry and political conditions in Israel, the U.S. and globally; the effect of tariffs on overall international trade and specifically on Kamada's ability to maintain expected sales and profit levels in light of such tariffs; the effect on the establishment and timing of business initiatives; Kamada's ability to leverage new business opportunities and integrate them with its existing product portfolio; unexpected results of clinical and development programs; regulatory delays; and other risks detailed in Kamada's filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (the "SEC"), including those discussed in its most recent Annual Report on Form 20-F and in any subsequent reports on Form 6-K, each of which is on file with, or furnished to, the SEC and available on…

Nine people, including the owner, family members and veterinary staff, were recommended to receive rabies post-exposure treatment after possible exposure to the infected animal's saliva. More than 40 cattle, a horse and three dogs are now under observation, while two unvaccinated barn cats with likely exposure were euthanized. BROWN COUNTY, Minn. (FOX 9) - The Minnesota Board of Animal Health confirmed a cow in Brown County tested positive for rabies on Sept. 8, prompting vaccines for nine people and quarantine measures for dozens of animals on the property. Cow with rabies in Minnesota Blanking More Often? Older Adults Are Rethinking This One ChoiceBrain Vitality Journal | SponsoredSponsored Undo Timeline: The owner first noticed the heifer behaving oddly on Sept. 1, when the animal was lying flat with its head down. A veterinarian examined the cow that same day, and the owner gave the animal oral medication with bare hands. The next day, a second veterinarian examined the heifer and also administered oral medication without wearing gloves. By Sept. 3, a third veterinarian examined the animal and found more serious symptoms — uncoordinated hind legs, high-stepping, vocalizing, excessive drooling and a high temperature. The animal was then humanely euthanized, and its head was sent for rabies testing at the Minnesota Department of Health (MDH) Public Health Laboratory, which confirmed the positive result on Sept. 8. What they're saying: "When we see livestock acting strangely, rabies may not be the first thing people think of to explain the behavior," said Dr. Steve Kivisto, senior veterinarian leading the rabies program at the Board. "Given the severity of the disease, it's better to assume an animal is infected until proven otherwise, and to be sure to take the proper precautions and use the correct personal protective equipment when working with a rabies suspect animal." "Consistent use of PPE when treating ill animals can help prevent exposure to rare illnesses such as rabies," said Dr. Stacy Holzbauer, State Public Health Veterinarian. "Additionally, MDH staff are available for consultation for any animal bite situation to assess rabies risk and provide recommendations for rabies prophylaxis." Who was exposed and what happens next What we know: MDH recommended nine people receive rabies post-exposure treatment, which involves human rabies immune globulin and a series of rabies vaccinations given at set intervals to prevent the disease from developing, according to the Board. Those recommended for treatment or rabies booster vaccinations include the owner, the owner's daughter, two minor children, two of the veterinarians who examined the animal and three veterinary technicians who assisted. While a bite from an infected animal is the most common way people are exposed to the rabies virus, the Board noted it is also important to wear gloves and eye protection to prevent saliva from entering the eyes, nose, mouth or an open wound when treating animals for an unknown neurological illness. On the property, the Board quarantined 13 cows, and more than 40 cattle are being kept under observation for rabies, according to the Board. A horse on the property was possibly exposed but is current on its rabies vaccinations and will be kept under observation, along with three vaccinated dogs. Two unvaccinated barn cats with likely exposure were euthanized. Numerous skunks were observed earlier this year on a neighboring plot of land owned by a relative that adjoins the area where the infected cow was kept, according to the Board. Skunks and bats are the natural carriers of rabies in Minnesota, and wild animals — especially bats — account for most of the state's annually reported rabies cases. Less than 15% of rabid animal cases reported each year in Minnesota involve domestic species, with cattle, cats and dogs being the most common. What we don't know: It has not been confirmed how the heifer was exposed to the rabies virus or which wild animal may have transmitted it. The Source: The Minnesota Board of Animal Health and the Minnesota Department of Health confirmed the rabies case and provided details on exposures, quarantine measures and prevention guidance. Kansans warned about increased rabies cases in bats and other animals

by Morgan Chilson, Kansas Reflector
September 16, 2026

TOPEKA — State health authorities warned Kansans to be aware of an increase in encounters with animals that carry rabies, primarily bats.

The Kansas Department of Health and Environment issued an advisory Tuesday urging health care providers to be aware of the importance of administering a rabies risk assessment because of increases in rabid animals.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention issued a similar advisory last week because many areas nationwide are reporting increased exposures to rabid or possibly rabid animals.

“Several high-profile rabies outbreaks and mass rabies exposure events have highlighted the importance of performing careful rabies risk assessments and following evidence-based recommendations for administering (post-exposure prophylaxis),” CDC’s advisory said.

Treatment for people exposed to rabies is a series of shots administered when rabies is suspected or confirmed. Rabies is nearly 100% fatal if treatment isn’t administered, the CDC advisory said.

KDHE encouraged health departments to help by reminding clinicians about the importance of administering a risk assessment before starting treatment. The assessment considers the risk of rabies in the animal, the circumstances that led to the exposure, if the animal had any clinical signs consistent with rabies, and the type and severity of the wound, the CDC advisory said.

There have been no human rabies cases in Kansas this year, according to the KDHE Infectious Disease Dashboard.

“Each year, 1.4 million Americans receive healthcare for a possible rabies exposure, 100,000 receive post-exposure prophylaxis, and fewer than 10 die from rabies due to robust prevention efforts,” a CDC report said.

The CDC received 17% more rabies-related inquiries from July through August, than during the same period in 2025.

The agency also received reports from at least eight state health departments of increased rabies post-exposure assessments being used.

“According to weekly pharmacy data as of September 2, 2026, utilization for the two rabies vaccines and the two rabies immunoglobulins licensed in the United States has increased by an estimated 33% and 76%, respectively, compared with the same time period last year,” a CDC report said.

Most rabies cases occur after wild animal exposures. KDHE data, updated as of June, found nine positive rabies cases in Kansas, with six cases in skunks, one in a cow, one in a dog and one in a bat.

Thirteen bats have tested positive for rabies in Montana this year. Riverstone Health says bat encounters are up this year. The county has tracked 11 incidents so far — eight of them involving human contact. That is already double the human interactions reported last year. Watch the full story below: Yellowstone County sees uptick in human interaction with bats 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE Stacie Pannell, communicable disease program manager at RiverStone Health, said an "interaction" does not always mean a bite. It can include a scratch — or even waking up in a room with a bat. "Were they bitten? Were they scratched? We don't know," Pannell said Friday. "After somebody has an interaction with a bat, we recommend post-exposure prophylaxis for rabies. That treatment is extensive. Pannell described what it involves. "They get immune globulin to start with. It's called HRAIG, or Human Rabies Immune Globulin, and the rabies vaccination. And then they get that rabies vaccination again on day three, seven, and fourteen," Pannell said. Pannell believes more people are reporting these encounters because awareness around rabies is growing. "I do think that it's made people more aware that bats do pose, or can pose, a danger for their health," Pannell said. Riley Buttram knows firsthand how painful that treatment can be. A bat bit her during a camping trip in 2018, and she describes the experience vividly. "It just felt like they were sticking a toothpick up my foot," Buttram said. "It was horrible." The bite happened in seconds. She reached into a car to grab a jacket. "I couldn't get it from one side of the car, so I went to the other side and grabbed it, and then I looked down and there was a bat, and it like bit me on my foot," Buttram said. She barely felt the bite, but she knew she could not ignore it. "We went to the hospital, and for precaution, they gave me seven shots in my foot because that's where it bit me," Buttram said. That was just the start. "Two of my thighs and two of my arms, and then they sent the bat off to get tested, and it did have rabies," Buttram said. The treatment was so intense that medical staff had to physically restrain her. "They had to hold me down because the needles are so long," Buttram said. Eight years later, Buttram still remembers it clearly — and she feels for those in Yellowstone County now going through the same thing. Her message is simple: don't take the risk. "If we wouldn't have kept the bat, we would have been like, 'Oh, okay, maybe she didn't get bit.' I would have gotten rabies. I could have died," Buttram said. Petting zoo goats test positive for rabies in North Carolina National Desk US LIVE Current Time 0:00 / Total Duration 2:16 Sorry, this video is not available, please check back later. Advertisement Updated: 5:23 PM EDT Sep 14, 2026 Editorial Standards i By Madison Czopek, PolitiFact Bat in your house? Rabid goat at the petting zoo? If exposed to rabies, what do you do? Updated: 5:23 PM EDT Sep 14, 2026 Editorial Standards i By Madison Czopek, PolitiFact In August, rabid beavers attacked park-goers in Maryland. Not long after that, more than 200 people in North Carolina were told to get rabies shots because baby goats at a mobile petting zoo exposed them to the deadly virus. This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com . Advertisement Frightening videos depicting violent animal attacks and news of rabies exposures seem to be all over social media lately. It’s not always clear if the animals involved have rabies, but in most cases the recommendation was the same: The victims needed rabies shots. Rabies is a serious viral disease that attacks the central nervous system and is almost always fatal in people after symptoms begin. Human cases are rare, but there are around 4,000 animal rabies cases each year, reported the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The most recent CDC data showed that from 2022 to 2023, there was a 5.1% increase in animal rabies cases. Although recent animal attacks and rabid animal anecdotes and warnings do not necessarily reflect quantitative trends, some public health officials say they have observed increases in animal attack reports this year. Idaho public health officials said the state found 24 rabid bats this year — more than in the past three years. In California’s San Diego County, public health authorities also documented an uptick in rabies-positive bats. The health director in Jones County, North Carolina, said the county has seen an abnormally high animal rabies case rate so far in 2026. None of the officials cited a potential cause. Here’s what doctors and wildlife experts want you to know about the threat. What animals carry rabies? All mammals can be infected with and transmit rabies, said Tanya LeRoith, the director of Virginia Tech’s Veterinary Teaching Hospital. Some animals, however, are more likely to carry rabies than others in the U.S., including bats, raccoons, skunks, foxes and mongooses. Symptoms of rabies in animals can include aggression, unsteady walking, weaving, spasms, rear-limb paralysis and difficulty swallowing. But any strange behavior or signs of illness can be a symptom of rabies in animals, LeRoith said. “Unfortunately it can be difficult to tell, especially if they seem friendly,” she said. Toby Talbot A tranquilized raccoon has its ear tagged by U.S. Department of Agriculture wildlife specialist Robert Acabbo in Grand Isle, Vt., Thursday, Sept. 27, 2007. When do I need a rabies vaccine? If an animal wounded you, clean the wound thoroughly with hot, soapy running water . Then, go to the nearest emergency department, Dr. Sean Grogan, an emergency medicine physician, told Yale Medicine News . Emergency room doctors will help assess your rabies risk and decide if you need rabies post-exposure prophylaxis, the scientific term for medical interventions that help prevent disease after someone is exposed to a virus like the one that causes rabies. If you’ve encountered a wild animal that was behaving strangely but it didn’t bite or scratch you and you are unsure if it’s a rabies risk, seek guidance from your state or local health department. Am I only at risk of rabies if an animal bites me? No. Rabies spreads through saliva, so bites are the biggest concern. But animals clean themselves often , meaning saliva can be all over their bodies. As a result, they can transmit the rabies virus even with a scratch . There’s also a risk of exposure through an open wound or any mucous membrane such as the mouth or eyes . “Consider a child feeds a baby goat, gets goat slobber on their hand, then puts their fingers in their mouth or their eyes,” said Dr. Meagan Deming, an infectious disease specialist and an expert with the University of Maryland’s Center for Vaccine Development and Global Health. “That’s an exposure.” Finding a bat in your house is also considered an exposure unless you are certain you were never in contact with it, she said. Bat teeth are so tiny that they can bite without you feeling it and without leaving a mark . “If you wake up to find a bat in your room? Exposure,” Deming said. “Child sleeping in a room and a bat was in there? Exposure.” That’s also true if someone is unable to say if they had contact with a bat either because of a disability or intoxication, she said. CDC issues alert about nationwide increase in rabies exposures What should I do if I think I have been exposed to rabies? Seek treatment as soon as possible. Medical personnel will clean and bandage any wounds and then you’ll likely get two injections: One that provides immediate antibodies and the first dose of what is typically a four-injection rabies vaccine series. It takes time for a vaccine to tell the immune system to make its own antibodies, so human rabies immune globulin, also called HRIG, helps people who haven’t been previously vaccinated begin fighting the virus right away. It is a biologic injection made from human donors who have high levels of rabies antibodies in their blood. It is administered close to the wound and given as soon as possible to stop the virus from attaching to the nervous system. After getting the first vaccine dose, you will return for additional doses on days three, seven and 14, according to CDC guidance . Immunocompromised adults need a fifth dose on day 28. If a medical provider documents a rabies exposure, Medicare , Medicaid and most health insurance companies typically cover the vaccine series, Deming said. The antibody injection can also be covered with the appropriate medical coding, but there are also patient assistance programs and people can consult the hospital or health department to find ways to cover the costs if needed, she said. Damian Dovarganes Dr. Kwane Stewart prepares a rabies vaccine for dogs of homeless people in the Skid Row area of Los Angeles on Wednesday, June 7, 2023. How can I reduce my chance of rabies exposure? Do not approach wild animals. Don’t feed them and don’t rescue them. “Leave that to the actual wildlife rescue societies,” Deming said. Get any pets or animals that frequently have human contact vaccinated against rabies. “The vaccine is very effective and infected pets can be a common cause of transmission to people if they are not vaccinated,” LeRoith said, adding that people should keep pets from interacting with wildlife if possible. (WITN) — Pitt County health officials are offering advice to pet owners after a stray cat tested positive for rabies this week, marking the county’s third confirmed case this year. County officials said the cat was found in the Mills Road area. One person encountered the animal and received treatment for rabies exposure. The incident follows positive rabies cases involving a fox and a raccoon in April. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, nationwide rabies case reports increased 17% in July and August compared to the same period last year. Pitt County Public Health Director Wes Gray noted that while there is an uptick, rabies cases remain rare in the community. “Well for the most part, even though we have cases, they still are rare,” Gray said. “We do see several a year and the last few years. And, we make sure the public is aware of those.” Veterinarian Dr. Fernanda Godfrey, of East Carolina Veterinary Service, emphasized that pet owners should treat rabies as an ongoing concern rather than reacting only when a new case surfaces. “Wild animals and the reservoirs for the rabies virus are constantly out there,” Godfrey said. “Pets can constantly be exposed to it. So, there is not really a seasonality to rabies exposure.” Health officials emphasize that the most effective way to protect pets is to ensure they remain current on rabies vaccinations. Gray warned residents never to touch or pet wild animals. For anyone exposed to a potentially rabid animal, Godfrey advises immediately washing the affected area with soap and water for at least 15 minutes to help prevent infection before seeking medical attention. To help protect local pets, Pitt County Animal Services offers $15 rabies vaccinations by appointment. (KY3) - The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is warning of an increase in reported rabies exposures across the country, and health officials say it is a reminder to take precautions at home. The warning comes as bats found in Greene County recently tested positive for rabies. Rabies is a virus that attacks the nervous system, and once symptoms appear, it is almost always fatal. CDC reports rise in exposures Last week, the CDC said eight different states have reported increases in people being exposed to rabid or potentially rabid animals since July. The agency did not say which states, but said it also received 17% more rabies-related inquiries from July through August than during the same time period last year. “It certainly gets your attention, but then it draws us back around to remember prevention and how important that is,” said Kendra Findley, BCBH program coordinator with the Taney County Health Department. Taney County has not had a confirmed case this year, but health officials say Missouri commonly sees rabies in bats and skunks. “We always warn people if they find a wild animal that’s acting sick or acting strangely, definitely do not approach it. I think that Missouri sees more rabies in skunks and bats than other animals, but still any warm-blooded animal can carry rabies,” Findley said. Warning signs and prevention This includes animals that may not immediately look sick. Health officials say unusual behavior, like a normally nocturnal animal being active during the day, aggression, or loss of balance, can be warning signs. That is why keeping pets vaccinated is important. “It’s absolutely critical. If you are a human being, any mammal that gets the rabies virus, if you start to show symptoms, it is nearly 100% fatal. You cannot come out of it,” said Cynthia Susanne with Animal Angels Network. Vaccinating pets can protect the animal, but it also creates another layer of protection for people. “We want exposure to make people understand that with that one shot, your dog has a chance to survive. Your cat has a chance to survive. And it does come from wildlife. We don’t want people being in fear of wildlife, of course, but that’s where it’s transmitted,” Susanne said. Seeking treatment Health officials say if someone is exposed, they should not wait to see if symptoms develop. The sooner someone gets evaluated, the better. “It’s incredibly crucial. As soon as you can get to speak to a healthcare provider, get assessed, that’s going to be important. Because again, once symptoms start, it is a fatal illness,” Findley said. Ashley has told stories all across the country, including in Maine, Central Pennsylvania and Tampa, where she won a Florida Association of Broadcast Journalists award in the "Multi-Media Journalist In a Large Market" category. Read Full Bio Ashley Paul Updated on: September 16, 2026 / 9:18 PM EDT / CBS Baltimore Add CBS News on Google The Harford County Health Department is warning parents after a bat found inside an elementary school in Bel Air, Maryland, tested positive for rabies. The rabid bat was found flying inside St. Margaret's Elementary School. It was submitted to the state laboratory on Sept. 1 and confirmed to be positive for rabies the following day. Health officials won't confirm or deny whether any students were injured by the bat. The bat is one of two bats and more than 22 animals in Harford County that have tested positive for rabies this year, according to the health department. Health officials are urging parents to talk with their children to determine whether they may have come into contact with the bat. "Parents should have a discussion with their children to determine if an exposure may have occurred. If the child touched a bat or the bat flew at them, we would recommend contacting their primary medical provider or the health department," the department said in a statement. The health department is also encouraging residents to take steps to keep wildlife out of their homes, including making sure doors close tightly, window screens are in place and any holes or openings leading from the outside are sealed. Harford County residents on alert The confirmed case inside an elementary school has some Harford County residents concerned about the presence of wildlife in the community. "There's a concern for sure that bats are in the school system to begin with, but I don't know what kind of system they have in place to check what's going on inside the building," Harford County resident Tim McGee said. "I have my grandkids who play outside and there's a lot of foxes and wildlife, so I'm concerned," added Harford County resident Anderson Lewis. The county health department is also continuing to distribute oral rabies vaccines as part of efforts to control the spread of rabies among wildlife, including raccoons and coyotes. Recent rabies cases across Maryland The Harford County case comes amid several other confirmed rabies cases involving wildlife across Maryland. Within the past two months, three people were attacked by beavers that later tested positive for rabies. Two incidents happened at Cunningham Falls State Park in Frederick County, while another occurred at Seneca Creek State Park in Montgomery County. The first Cunningham Falls incident involved 13-year-old Dominick Cebula. His father, Jeff Cebula, said his son was looking at fish in a creek when a beaver latched onto his chest. "He grabbed its head and a leg, and he tried to get it off of him, but at that point, he kind of felt that it was locked onto him," Jeff Cebula told WUSA9 in Washington, D.C. "And then it started shaking its head kind of like a dog would do." The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has also reported an increase in rabies-related inquiries during the summer. Advertisement Updated: 4:53 PM EDT Sep 14, 2026 Editorial Standards i Carrie Hodgin 12th case of rabies reported in Guilford County after cat tests positive Updated: 4:53 PM EDT Sep 14, 2026 Editorial Standards i Carrie Hodgin GUILFORD COUNTY, N.C. — The Guilford County Health and Human Services Agency and the Department of Public Health are warning people in the county about another rabies case. RABIES CASE REPORTED The county reported its twelfth confirmed case of rabies for the year, after a cat on Bailiff Street in Greensboro tested positive for the rabies virus on Monday. Advertisement Get the latest news stories of interest by clicking here RABIES VACCINATION AND NC LAW North Carolina law requires that all pets (cats, dogs and ferrets), whether living inside or outside, aged four months or older be vaccinated for rabies. Pets that are in outdoor fenced areas should also have current rabies vaccinations. Guilford County Animal Services may be contacted for more information on rabies prevention at 336-641-2506 or visit www.guilfordcountync.gov/animalservices . Keep up with the latest news and weather by downloading the WXII app here . Rabies circulates within the wildlife population throughout the entire year. Here are some tips to help prevent you or your family from being exposed to the rabies virus: Avoid direct contact with wildlife, dead or alive. Do not approach, try to play with, touch, rescue or treat any wildlife. If you find a sick or injured animal, contact Animal Control at 336-641-5990. Avoid any animal displaying unnatural behavior. Wild animals are not usually friendly so be very careful if they approach you. Do not try to separate fighting animals. Feed your pets indoors. Leaving food outside will attract dogs, cats and other wildlife into your yard. Report all stray animals to Animal Control at 336-641-5990 in Greensboro and 336-883-3224 in High Point. Stray animals may not have current rabies vaccinations. If a person is bitten by an animal (domestic or stray), wash the bitten area immediately with soap and water, seek medical attention, and report the bite to local Animal Control Officers. supplementary_news.content: Another bat tests positive for rabies in rural Harney County HARNEY COUNTY-Public health officials have issued an alert after another bat tested positive for rabies in rural Harney County. The specific location of the encounter within the county has not been released. According to a public advisory from the Harney County Health Department and High Country Health and Wellness Center, the animal was recently discovered alive, alone, and exhibiting signs of illness in a local driveway. A private citizen safely secured the bat inside a sealed glass container before transporting it to a local veterinarian. The specimen was subsequently frozen and sent to the Oregon Public Health Laboratory, where diagnostic testing confirmed the presence of the rabies virus. Health authorities confirmed there is no known human or animal exposure associated with this incident. However, officials are taking the opportunity to remind the public that handling wild animals poses severe health risks. Public Health Recommendations To prevent potential exposure to rabies—a fatal but preventable viral disease—the health department advises residents to take the following precautions: Avoid Direct Contact: Never handle a bat, whether it appears sick, injured, or dead. Never handle a bat, whether it appears sick, injured, or dead. Vaccinate Pets: Keep dogs, cats, and other domestic pets up to date on all rabies vaccinations. Keep dogs, cats, and other domestic pets up to date on all rabies vaccinations. Secure Buildings: Seal external openings and ensure window screens are intact to keep bats from entering living spaces. Seal external openings and ensure window screens are intact to keep bats from entering living spaces. Act Quickly on Exposure: Wash any potential bite or scratch immediately with soap and water, then seek medical attention or contact public health officials right away. For inquiries or to report potential bat exposures, contact the Harney County Health Department at 541-573-2271. Additional information can be found through the Oregon Health Authority and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

(WBTV) - South Carolina has already reported several rabies cases this year, including seven cases in York County. A new case involving a bat is now putting a spotlight on what people should know if they encounter wildlife. At least 81 cases have been reported across the Palmetto State so far this year. Chris Shomo with A-1 Wildlife Control said the threat of rabies can come from where you least expect it. “Sometimes bats can come down in through chimneys. They usually don’t roost or live in there because it’s too slick on the inside, but when they do come in there, they usually end up at the bottom, inside the home because they don’t have anywhere else to go,” Shomo said. York County is now just two cases away from matching last year’s reports. “When it comes to certain species and types of animals, there’s definitely risk of you know, infectious disease, diseases, whether that be from contracting something from a bite or a scratch or direct contact with an animal,” Shomo said. South Carolina’s Department of Health says raccoons, skunks, foxes and bats are the main carriers of rabies in the state. It also says it’s not always easy to tell when you or a pet has been bitten by a bat because their teeth are so small. “If the bat can be contained, taken away by animal control, they will test it for rabies. They will get a positive or a negative. If it’s negative you’re in the clear. If it’s positive, even if you don’t know that you’ve been exposed or bitten,” Shomo said. “They probably are going to want you and urge you very much to get a series of shots and injections.” To prevent rabies, the department says, don’t keep wild animals as pets, avoid touching wild or stray animals with bare hands, vaccinate your pets and watch for strange behaviors in animals. Shomo says don’t ignore signs of animals in your home. “Don’t assume just because you stopped hearing it for a few days that it went away on its own. Animal issues just don’t resolve themselves,” Shomo said. “If you haven’t located where it’s happening and gotten rid of the animal and trapped it and seal the area up, that issue was going to persist.” If you do come into contact with a wild or unvaccinated animal, reach out to animal control or a wildlife professional for help. supplementary_news.content: 3 rabid animals found in South Carolina; 6 people, 7 pets exposed Ad (30s) Ad Watch: 9.16 WYFF News 4 Morning Headlines 9.16 WYFF News 4 Morning Headlines WYFF US LIVE Current Time 0:00 / Total Duration 6:22 Sorry, this video is not available, please check back later. Advertisement Updated: 1:26 PM EDT Sep 16, 2026 Editorial Standards i Zach Rainey Digital Content Producer 3 rabid animals found in South Carolina; 6 people, 7 pets exposed Updated: 1:26 PM EDT Sep 16, 2026 Editorial Standards i Zach Rainey Digital Content Producer ANDERSON COUNTY, S.C. — South Carolina health officials have confirmed that three animals from different counties have tested positive for rabies. Six people and seven pets have been exposed. Anderson County In Anderson County, a skunk found near Daniel Drive and Williford Road in Anderson tested positive for rabies. One person was potentially exposed and has been referred to their healthcare provider. Advertisement The skunk in Anderson County was the ninth rabid animal reported countywide in 2026. Horry County In Horry County, a stray cat found near Hendricks Short Cut Road and Zaccheus Lane in Conway tested positive for rabies. Two people were exposed and have been referred to their healthcare providers. Two cats and one dog were exposed and will be quarantined as required in the Rabies Control Act. Officials said that several stray cats in the area may have also been exposed, and local animal control is actively assisting with assessing and managing these animals to reduce further risk. The cat in Horry County was the county's first rabid animal reported this year. York County In York County, a bat found near Lometa Drive and Waterside Trail in York tested positive for rabies. Three people were exposed and have been referred to their healthcare providers. Two cats and two dogs were exposed and will be quarantined as required in the Rabies Control Act. The bat was the seventh rabid animal confirmed in York County this year. All three animals were submitted to the South Carolina Department of Public Health's laboratory for testing on Thursday, Sept. 10, and were confirmed to have rabies Friday, Sept. 11. Statewide, South Carolina has reported 86 rabid animals in 2026. Since 2002, the state has averaged about 136 rabies cases annually. In 2025, South Carolina recorded 101 confirmed cases, including 11 in Anderson County, three in Horry County, and nine in York County. I Believe I Was Exposed to Rabies, What Should I Do? If you believe you, someone you know, or your pets have come in contact with this skunk, cat, bat, or another animal that potentially has rabies, please call DPH's rabies 24-hour rabies reporting line at (888) 847-0902 (Select Option 2). What is a Rabies Exposure? An exposure is defined as direct contact (such as through broken skin or mucous membranes in the eyes, nose, or mouth) with saliva or brain/nervous system tissue from an infected animal. Be sure to immediately wash any part of your body that may have come in contact with saliva or neural tissue with plenty of soap and water and seek medical attention.
